As this device must be assembled before putting into the tank, it is advisable first to make s brass plate which need not be round, but can be most easily turned up in• that form. In this put two holes tapped to take the pet cocks. Before placing the pet cocks make each of them into three-way cocks by drilling a hole into the side and through one side of the valve; then set the cocks in the brass disc with the side holes adjoining. Force between the two cocks a short piece of tube and solder it thoroughly all the way around. This makes a by-pass between the two. The device is now ready to be soldered in place in the tank with the two cocks set in position. The petrol will flow through the supply pipe as long as it is above the level of the standpipe, and when it has gone below that point, turn the cocks to allow the petrol to flow through the main supply pipe until the tent is empty. It will be readily understood that the auxiliary pipe may also be used as a drain pipe. On refilling the tank be sure to turn the cocks back into position. LOOK AFTER YOUR CLUTCH.

The motor cyclist should never forget that the clutch is a very delicate piece of mechanism. If treated well it will work successfully for a long time, but if abused in any way it is simply bound to give trouble in a short time. Here are a few rules that ought to be observed by every clutch- motor-cycle owner. Get the maker's instructions off by heart and obey them religiously. If he tells you to use thin oil, use thin oil and no other. It may seem that thick oil would be better in summer at least, but the maker knows best. Never have a clutch in the "out position for more than a few minutes at a time. It weakens the spring. Don't run far with the clutch slipping or too slack; if you do undue wear takes place. Also don't run with the adjustment too tight; this strains the machine. Handle your clutch controls as gingerly as you handle the gas and air levers. _

div.p: RUSSIAN CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS.

A resolution forwarded to.. the -Warrington Trades and Labour Council by the Committee of the Russian Socialist Groups in London was read on Tuesday evening. It called upon. Brit- ish organised workers to use all the means in their power for the protection of the right of asylum in Great Britain, and prevention of any attempt to deport to Russia all Russians of mili- tary age unwilling to enlist in the Britit Army.—The Chairman asked if anyone wished to propose the resolution, and there was no re- sponse for some time, until Mr. Howard moved its adoption, saying that some would be glad to
get out of England and get refuge in some other countries.--The motion was carried.

div.head: UNION BANK OF MANCHESTER.
div.p: UNION BANK OF MANCHESTER.
Remarkable National And tocal War- Time Prosperity.

The eightieth annual general meeting of the Union Bafix of Manchester, Limited, was held at the Head Office of the Bank, York-street, Manchester, on Friday last week. Mr. G. C. Haworth, presiding and moving the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, spoke of the way in which, our trade has been maintained during the war. Referring to freights, he said that in normal times the price for bringing freight across the Atlantic was id. per lb.; now the charges, including in- surance, were anything from four to six times greater. Notwithstanding this charge, and the increased cost of production, they found the cotton trade balance sheets declaring dividends. The present price of middling American cotton was just over Bd. per pound; two years ago it was 41d. To-day's pike of 811 b. shirtings is 9s. 6d.; in 1914 it was 7s. 3d. The prosperity of the Yorkshire woollen industry stood out above all others in the extent of orders and margins of profit and in prices. Deliveries were eighteen months in arrear. The prices of woollen goods were 100 per cent. higher; the cost of dyeing was increased from 100 to 300 per cent. beyond the rates quoted in 1913. Our merchant business, whether for home or export, had on the whole been satisfactory. The reason for this was that the United Kingdom and many markets abroad are almost solely dependent upon the production of the English manufac- turer for all textiles. To all intents and pur- poses, the exportation of goods from France, Switzerland and Germany has practically ceased. In the building trade we find a stag- nant coiidition of things, altogether without parallel. Nevertheless, the very material they use—timber—shows an advance of from 100 to 300 per cent. Agriculture, once regarded as an unremunerative calling, has participated in ex- ceptional demands arising from the war, and to an extent that the most sanguine had no reason to expect. Cattle, corn and hay have advanced from 50 to 150 per cent. The heavy cost of the war has one feature to which he would draw attention. Whether you take trade locally or nationally, the fact remains that the money paid out in loans circu- lates round to the banker, the merchant, and the shopkeeper. This naturally gives an in- centive to our home trade. •

Controversialists might dispute about Britain's part in the war, but no one would question the fact that British money power, British credit, and British economic strength, combined with an all-powerful fleet, was the great prop and stay of the Allied cause. Since August, 1914, the banks have been united in their action on behalf of the national cause, and they had had little or no difficulty in recon- ciling it with their duty to their shareholders, their depositors, and their customers: The past two years would be looked upon in future as the most remarkable period in the history of British banking. Reviewing the balance sheet of the bank, Mr. Haworth said there had been a larger net profit than on any previous occasion, which had en- abled them to pay the usual dividend without deducting income tax, which was equivalent to a considerable increase of dividend. The total of the balance sheet, £9,683,985, exceeded the total of 1915 by more than a million sterling. The bank had now attained a remarkably strong position, its business showed great vitality, and the directors thought there was a future before it which would yield satisfaction to all con- nected. Mr. W. H. Verdin seconded and the motion was carried.
Sir Joseph Verdin and Sir Charles ,Behrens were re-elected directors.

CYCLING AND MOTORING.
THE WAY TO FIT A NEW SPOKE.

It is a very rare occurrence to break a spoke on a reliable cycle, but now and then it does happen. On a cheap mount it is naturally more common, since poorer material is used in the manufacture of the machine. Some of our roads are in such a shocking state of repair at the present moment that the surprising thing is that broken spokes are so rare. As a rule, the fact that a spoke is broken is not discovered until one is cleaning the machine, but immediately the fact is discovered a repair should be executed right away, or the accuracy of the wheel may become affected. The fitting of a new spoke is not a job to frighten anyone. It isn't even necessary to take the wheel out, unless it hap- pens to be a spoke fitting into the free wheel aide of the back wheel. You must take off the tyre and tube, uncouple the tape that keeps the tube from, chafing on the rim, and draw out the broken spoke. Then carefully ascertain the length of the spoke re- quired either by measuring the old one or one of the others in position, and by'one just a fraction of an inch longer (1-16th of an inch longer is enough), but of precisely the same gauge. Better buy a new nipple (the little nut that holds the spoke in the rim), as it is ten to one against the old nipple fit- ting the new spoke. Thread the spoke first through the hole in the hub, then through the hole in the rim, screw on the nipple and tighten it up to a tension equal to that of the others, prkferably by means of a spoke nipple key. If you have not one of these you can use a small pair of pliers. Better test the wheel for truth afterwards by spinning it round and holding a bit of chalk against the forks so that it just does not touch the rim. If a chalk mark shows on the rim here and there, obviously the wheel does not spin true.- Then you must file dciwn the rim end of the spoke flush with the nipple top before replacing the tube, or else you are sure to have a lot of trouble with punctures.

div.head: LOYALTY TO PRAYER.
div.p: LOYALTY TO PRAYER.
Father Chamberlain's Striking Appeal _ _
At St. Alban's.

"Call. upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver thee and thou shalt glorify Me,., was the strikingly appropriate text chosen by the Rev. W. A. Chamberlain, who preached to a large congregation at St. Alban's Roman Catholic Church, Bewsey-street, on Sunday. Referring to the second anniversary of Eng- land's participation in the European War, he said it was a time for neither undue optimism or excessive pessimism. At a moment such as this it was well to consider why God permitted such an evil to' afflict the human race. The old Catholic view that war, pestilence and plague were direct punishment for sin should never be forgotten. Alongside with the advance, during the last century of man's conquest of material nature had been a growing tendency among men to take satisfaction in their own skill to the exclusion of God. The glorification of man's power led him to leave.. God out of .his life. So God permitted this war to show man his weak- ness. He pleaded for, all to unite in earnest prayer. Many were prevented by age, sex or occupation from actively helping their country in this hournf need, but :all could, and. should show their duty to God and their loyalty to their country by zeal in prayer. The British people believed in the justice and righteousness of their cause. So they had no need to fear to plead before the .good God. The horrors and sufferings of these times ought to excite devo- tion; while all in these days of universal ser- vice had particular and personal requests to make to God. Many, too, needed prayer to ob- tain that resignation and consolation so neces- sary in this sad season. In concluding, the preacher asked each one to examine himself and see what extra or special effort he was making in prayer in these times. That night a 'special act of adoration before the Blessed Sacrament was being made in union with all the churches throughout the Archdiocese of Liverpool to pray for victory and lasting peace.

div.head: REV. A. M. M.
div.p: THE REV. A. M. M.
Buttonwood Vicar's Racy View Of His Health And Age.
--With sprightly literary gait, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell pens the following paragraphs concern- ing himself in his "Parish Magazine" this month—

div.head: DELIGHTFUL!
div.p: DELIGHTFUL!

Don't you think this is delightful? People are saying of us (us is the parson), "Why, he's looking splendid, younger than when he first came (a matter of a quartet cen- tury only) and as lively as a kitten!"
A finer- Compliment Could not be paid to any- one, priest or layman; we of course accept it and—believe it speaks the truth. Herein is evidence of the truth of the Gospel I " Never grow old!"
"I'm never going to be old, never, never; I'm going to be young for ever and ever."

People. marvel, "What, no glasses yet!" "And no dental adornment" ('twere too brutal to say "false teeth")! "Your way of living;" say the critics, "must he the right way; we're all coming round, preparing to fall into line." • Delightful, is it not? . .- -

A wee stretch of our vivid local imagination will picture the buried parson of Burtonwood standing on a pedestal at Bridge Foot! Well! Active! Young! Still going strong! Without flesh meat; without hicohol; without tobacco!

Perpetual youth is no dream; it is a fact somewhere, anyhow! , If we go on, as now, a wee bit longer we may expect in due time to reach the 'forties! Imagine being in the 'forties (over 41 for obvious military reasons) ,at a time when we are not deemed too old at sixty, or even seventy! Will wonders ever cease?

div.head: COLONEL'S PRAISE FOR WARRINGTON BOYS.
div.p: COLONEL'S PRAISE FOR WARRINGTON BOYS.

The first ten days of the Grammar School holidays were, quite appropriately, devoted by the School Cadet Corps in taking part in the practical work of camp life. One of the boys, acting as war correspondent for "The Ex- aminer," writes at the conclusion of hostilities as follows:

On July 28, 85 members of the Grammar School Cadet Corps, in charge of Captain_ Pear- son and Lieut. Pape, left Warrington to spend ten days in camp at Chatsworth Park. We formed a unit of the North-Western Section Schools Camp, the object of which was to com- bine military training with a pleasant holiday. , There were nearly 400 boys altogether in tie I camp, in charge of The 0.C., Captain Hillier, of Liverpool, and the Adjutant, Captain Pear- son. We found the organisation splendid, special attention being paid to the catering and for the care of the sick. The cooks were ex- perienced men from ships, and there were few complaints about either the quality or quantity of the food. At the close of camp the boys showed their appreciation for their efforts by raising a substantial sum for them. The serving of the meals was under the super- vision of the Battalion Sergeant-Major, who hay seen service in South Africa. The sick were attended by a local .doctor, who _motored over every morning. The hot weather was respon- sible for a few cases of slight sunstroke, and these were accommodated in a special hospital tent.

We could not complain of being overworked, for we were dismissed at 3.30 p.m. every day. Cricket and football were the chief diversions, while Am the evenings concerts were arranged, in which" officers, and cadets took part -Our two Sundays in camp were made notable by the presence at the church parades of the Bishops of Derby and Southwell. . Our military training mostly took the form of "attack and defence," for which the • hilly nature,of the, ground was highly suitable. Of the route marches, the most interesting was to Haddon Hall, through which the cadets were taken.

div.head: FROM HATRED TO LOVE.
div.p: FROM HATRED TO LOVE.
Rector Remembers The Crimea And National Anger.

Preaching a notable sermon on the war, the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), at the Parish Church on Sunday evening, recalled with especial gratitude the change in our relatifins with Russia. He •remembered the time when the Crimean War raged, he said, and could not forget the anger and hatred then existing, be- tween the two nations. "We know Russia better now," remarked the Rector in a sentence of moving sincerity. "We are beginning to see what splendid qualities her people have, what magnificent soldiers and what devoted soldiers they are." The Rector said they had great cause for thankfulness for the magnificent response the men and women of England had made in the cause of justice, liberty and freedom. Splen- did voluntary service had been given by mil- lions of men and women either in civil life or in the Army; and willingness to pay their just proportion, in taxes, towards the war was mani- fest. Some people, they knew, had made money during the war, but others had suffered terribly. Landed proprietors, in many cases, hardly knew what to do, and yet they had not for a moment objected to pay their fair share towards the £5,000,010 a day which the war was costing. In conclusion the Rector remarked upon the problems which will face us at the conclusion of the, war, and said it was a cause for thank- fulness that our rulers were already taking counsel and making wise provision to meet the industrial and economic difficulties which might occur,

div.head: OVERSHADOWS EVERYTHING.
div.p: OVERSHADOWS EVERYTHING.
The Rev. T .T.. James On The Omnipresence Of The War.

The Rev. T. T. James took for his 'text- "The land we from our fathers had in trust" when he preached in ,Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday evening to a large congre- gation. He observed that that day was being kept as a day of special memory. It was the nearest Sunday to that day on which two years ago they realised the tremendous impost of the European struggle by their own ils.ry into it. There was.a period during which he wondered whether it would he wise to leave the conflict, which was so much present with them, an] endeavour to devote attention to other matters as they met there week by week for worship-- , whether it would give them rest and relief to turn to something else. Her 'had ,come to thq conclusion that whether it was desirable or not, it was impossible. "We have met." he added, "each Sabbath for two years with this shadow over us, and it has always made its presence felt. All religious questions lead up to i at 'last: all spiritual truth has to be looked at from the aspect'of the war. To think ourselves back again into the pre-war period grows in- creasingly difficult, and those days will never return. It is our business and our duty now to be facing the problems which will be with us when the war is over, and to be meeting the present and immediate issue of the conflict it- self with courage and .with faith. If we felt it to be right to engage in this war at the be- ginning, if we felt we colild do no other with honour and with loyalty to-our principles and ideals, nothing has happened since which' has given us cause to alter that opinion- Every new revelation of the meaning of the struggle, and every new vision of the issues involved, has tended to strengthen our conviction of the just- ness of our cause.

div.head: SURPRISED OUR FOES.
div.p: SURPRISED OUR FOES.

Rev. W. T. Derry On The Backbone Of England. Rev. W. T. Derry, preaching at Bewsey-road WeSleyan Church, struck a note of triumphant encouragement. Having expounded his text, Luke xxi., 28, ", Look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draweth nigh," he said in these critical times• the corps of encouragers can render their country the greatest service. 'Munitions, money, men," but the greatest of these is men, and all alike depend on the spirit that animates the rank and file of the British people. And if we can give a reason for the hope that is in us, then our well-grounded hope beComes a contagious and conquering confidence, and we can make no mean contrbution to the resoluteness, the patience, the courage of our fellow-countrymen. If cowardice is contagious, so is courage. The most inspiring literature produced to-day is not in the newspapers but in the letters from the lads at the Front, and the most cheerful faces and voices are not in our homes, but our hos- pitals. If they are in, such good heart, surely we aliould be. We have good reason for thanks- giving. The more it is considered by ourselves and neutral nations, the more clearly our cause is seen to be the cause of truth and justice and freedom. We should be grateful for our de- liverance from invasion, starvation and serious defeat., The Navy has kept our shores almost inviolate,, and has safeguarded our supplies of food and necessities, which have come to us from far off lands in sufficient, if not ample, measure. The food on our tables to-day is proof conclusive that tb-?, battle of Jutland was a British victory, and every one in Germany must know it from Kaiser to corner boy. We should be thankful that our now armies have shown that their courage is equal to all de- mands. They, have surprised their foes and convinced them that the British race has back- bone still.

• Let us give thanks that the necessary sacri- fices have not been grudged by those who have given husbands and sons and brothers. The latter have in many cases made the great sacri- fice, the former have made the greatest sacrifice, giving up what was dearer to them than life. The measure of their sacrifice tells us how much they love liberty, how much they love their country.

Let us be grateful that industry has been suc- cessfully mobilised and that labour • troubles have been trivial and few. It was not a small thing that was asked of the working- men when they were requested to forego for the duration of the War their hard, won rights; but when it was -pointed out that the soldiers had ;,given up far more and were quite helpless ' without them. and unless their efforts were unceasing and the utmost of which 'thej, were Capabte, then they showed that the men in the works were of the same breed as the men in the war, and that they would stand by their brothers and their country to the end.

Let us be 'thankful ,that our Allies have been faithful. In joining Germany, Austria, Turkey and Bulgaria have yielded to her leadership and submitted to her control. But we and our Allies have united Our forces on equal terms.

_ And let - -us be grateful that thiA tide has turned and ,time is ,fighting for us. With our superiority in means and men, if we relax no effort, the third year of the war should see its close and the accomplishment of the objects for which we were compelled to strive. Certainly we have every reason to "look up and lift up our heads." Because our cause is just and our motives pure we have the Tight to pray for victory if we ask in submissjon to the will of Him Who is Wisdom and Power, Purity and Love.

div.head: STORIES OF THE WAR.
div.p: STORIES OF THE WAR.
HATTON MAN ENJOYS STRAFING SNIPERS WITH GRENADES.

Lance-Corporal Herbert Leach, of Hatton, writing on July 23rd to his brother, Mr. F. Leach, 75, Walton-road, Stockton Heath, from France, records his experiences in the firing line, in support trenches and in reserve. You will be surprised to hear,:' he says, "that the time I enjoyed best was when I was in the firing line. I had a sort of roving com- mission, letting the Huns have a few rifle grenades: We made a speciality of snipers. As a rule the medicine proved very effective, as they were quite good for a time after we had ' strafed ' them. I hope to have this job when we go up again, as it is very interesting work. .

"Nothing has happened sinca we came here. This is what they call a 'quiet part' of the line, but you would hardly think so when the artillery starts and rifle grenades and aerial darts are flying about. . . . . We rarely see a newspaper. For this reason I should be glad if you would let me have the weekly edition of a daily paper or a local newspaper sccasionally."
" GOT " A FEW OF THE ENEMY HIMSELF.

Sergeant Herbert Chile, of the -Royal Scots, late of 9, Robson-street, who is wounded, as already recorded ,in "The Examiner," and is now in a Birmingham hospital,'write S to a friend to say that he is "doing fine." "I got hit with a nosecap of a Hun shell— nowt very serious. My equipment saved me a lot; broken ribs and injuries below the belt (in- ternal), but I am getting on fine. . . . We were in reserve to a brigade that got stuck in the centre, and off we went to support. What a, rush! We took all before us in the German front line, and advanced right through. Our gunners are superb. What a difference to last year. Our artillery are it as well the Huns know; no -wonder 'they are all more or less de- mented after bombardment. . . . We did not get off free—can't expect—but I know most of the casualties will soon be fit again. We fairly enjoyed the fun—short, but exciting. The boys were splendid, singing, cracking jokes and ` strafing ' very much the same time. . . . The German position is strong, but we shall win. The pigs,-Bavarian and Prussian, 'hands up' when we do get into them—it is up to us every time now. . . . I don't Mind goini
through the same dose again. I got a few of the pigs myself. They walked into it About a month and I'll be going again."

div.head: HARD TIMES AND GOOD TIMES; NOT SO BAD ALTOGETHER.
div.p: HARD TIMES AND GOOD TIMES; NOT SO BAD ALTOGETHER.

Mr. Benjamin Farrar, 5, Willis-street, has received the following letter from Mr. J. Oxley, a member of the Wycliffe P.S.A., who is at present on active service in France:— " I suppose you have read all about the great push (rather good). It was a glorious sight on the first of July. I was quite near to tho front line, and was able to witness the opening stages of the big fight. I don't mind telling you that I had to perform a few tricks when it got tGo hot. I always managed to land in my under- ground villa.. What a game! It would make a rabbit laugh if one could only catch a glimpse of us trying to rush down our dug-outs. A Narrow Escape.

"Three of us had a rafher narrow escape ow. morning. We were going through a ruined village when a big shell came over- and burst on the other side of the road along which we were walking. None of us were hit. 'lt was a stroke of luck not being hit by the splinters of the shell. I couldn't help but laugh the way the three of us tried to sccamble behind a 'ruined house. Of course, that is only one of the incidents which occur out here. "We have hard times and we have good ff times,' so taking thin gh all round life o active service isn't very bad. The time came for us to leave our dug-outs and go behind the lines for a week or so. What a change,! It took me two days to serape the mud off my clothes. I got over that all right, and now I am in a peace- ful little village.

div.head: Contrast.
div.p: A Contrast.

"I was walking past a school this afternoon and I heard the scholars singing. They were singing the National Anthems of the Allies. They sang the French and Belgian anthems in their own language, and, of course, I expected to hear ours sung in French, but I got a sur- prise, for they commenced singing "Tipperary" in English, and good English too. What a change. Last week I was listening to the roar of the heavy guns, and to-day listening to the singing of those happy little refugees, They
are happy because they know that before long they will be able to go back to their own little villages and homes., That is' what I am patiently wAiting for. Eager For P.S.A. Meetings.

"I should have come on leave last month, but this ' Push ' stopped all leave. I don't mind, for in time we will all be coming home for good. You say that the P.S.A. meetings are very thin. Well, Mr. Farrar, you know that although the lads are not attending the P.S.A. meeting, they are attending a big meeting out here, and I am sure when this affair is settled you will see' the lads will be only too pleased to help to fill Wycliffe P.S.A. every Sunday afternoon and make it a success as it has always been.

"Mr. James has seen a bit of life out here, and he will tell you that the lads are eager to attend a meeting at the Y.M.C.A. and other places whenever they get the chance. It is im- possible to hold meetings too near the trenches, because Fritz always raises an objection to large gatherings. "I hope all the brothers have the good luck to return safe and sound when the war is ow.r. With the best of wishes to you and all the brothers, and may the Wycliffe P.S.A. be a great success in the future !"

div.head: LAY PREACHER ARRESTED. Alfred Walker Handed Over To
div.p: LAY PREACHER ARRESTED. Alfred Walker Handed Over To
Military Authorities.

The little room in the Offices of Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co., Winwick-street, which serves as a County Occasional Court, was crowded with spectators on Monday, when Alfred Walker, a lay preacher at the Working Men's Mission, and residing at 98, Liverpool-road, was charged with failing to report himself under the 31ilitary Service Act. Walker was arrested on Saturday. It was stated that he had appealed on conscientious grounds to the Warrington Rural Tribunal and the Liverpool Appeal Court, but his case had been dismissed. A notice summoning him to present himself for service on the 17th July was sent him on the 14th, but, apart from ack- nowledging it, he had not observed its instruc-' tions.

P.C. Phillips • said that when .he went to arrest the prisoner on Saturday he. was asked: "Have you come to arrest .me?" Witness re-, plied "Yes," and took him to the Sankey Police Station. A gentleman in the Court asked if he might be allowed to say something, but the Chairman (Councillor Henry Roberts) replied that he did not think they could hear him. There seemed to be a mistaken impression that when those cases came before the Court the whole question of conscience could be re-argued.. The magis- trates' duty was more of an administrative than a. judicial one. They were not concerned as to why the prisoner did not appear, having no alternative but to make the order for him to be handed over to the military authorities. They had to refuse to listen to arguments on that point. The Prisoner: Is the prisoner allowfd to say anything? The Chairman pointed out that he had ad- mitted the offence. Mr. Thomas Dale then asked whether Mr. Walker's wife would be allowed to see him 'while he remained in Warrington, and the Chairman remarked that facilities of a reason- able and proper kind would be granted. The order for the handing over to the mili- tary having been made, with the addition of a fine of 405., Mr. Dale said: "May I make a protest as a member of the Mission to which he belongs?" The Chairman: You are not concerned in the matter. Outside the Court I could appreciate what you say, but inside I have no power. The Bench then rose and the Court was cleared.

ECONOMICS AFTER THE WAR.

Sir,—Continuing the subject of my last letter we find that, from almost every civilised coun- try, comes news of preparations for the great economic struggle which must inevitably follow the conclusion of the present war. We are daily confronted with particulars of the mani- fold efforts of the Central Empires to prepare for peace, and if they do it as efficiently as their preparations for war their competition will be formidable. Other nations, too, see the cataclysm in Europe has created an entirely new position, and are looking forward with confidence to being able to play a more im- portant part in the commercial and industrial world. There is no room for complacency in view of the prospects that lie before the manu- facturers and exporters of this country, after Peace is declared. After the war conditions will •be greatly changed, and it is quite obvious that we shall have to organise our economic and industrial resources. The business community alone can- not accomplish the change, but must be sup- ported by Government and by labour; the -union of these three may lead on to success. With an enormous debt on which interest must he Paid, with our hold on foreign securities Featly reduced, the country will only be able r Pay its way by restricting the value of its .imports or increasing the value of its exports. That can only be done by producing goods, distributing goods and selling goods at prices comparable with those which rule in other countries. The resources of the British Empire are boundless, and in spite of the cost of the war British credit ensures that capital will be available if it can be shown that the other two la.ctors will also accomplish their part—the co- oPeration of executive ability, capital and labour. It will be the duty of the executive Portion of the community to organise our Inanufacturing industries, our banks, our trans- Port system, and our selling arrangements, so that in all these matters we shall be at least as efficient as any other nation. Mr. Bigland says:' "To-day it is the people, not the politicians, who see visions, and who have no use for any leader without the pene- tration and the genius to materialise these visions into concrete opportunities for them- selves and their fellow-subjects in the Empire; into Acts of Parliament framed on Imperial lines, with the prosperity of the Empire as an end; into Budgets that will benefit the Empire and the nations who reciprocate and penalise enemy countries." He further argues: "It 332ay be well forthwith to dispose of an objec- tion which is sure to be raised, that counter- barriers to our proposed duties would be erected, operating to the detriment of ourselves and our Allies. To those timid ones who cry If I hit him he may hit me back,' I would reply: Make no mistake, he will hit if he ea; whether you hit him or not; hit him, therefore, so hard that he cannot.' In other Words, the economic weapons we hold, notably In the matter of raw materials, are far more Powerful than anything in the armoury of the enenif. Refuse to use these weapons and Ger- Many will soon be in the same position as she would be on the seas if we refused to let the British Navy out of harbour. The Allies can get on without Gerintin supplies, but the con- veree does not hold; so that if we will but use it the whip hand is ours." Reform is necessary in all our methods of Procedure and even in our outlook in life. Re- form in our banking in our shipping, in our trading, in our consular service,. and.pur..com- rnercial procedure. We must cease to- be the -simple commercial entrepot and inter- national clearing-house for the world's commerce. We must be something more than this. If we are simply the carriers and bankers of the world, if. we simply handle the products of others, we are on the highway to becoming divided into two distinct parties—the very rich and the very Poor; our working class will be on the way to become simply hewers of wood and drawers of Water to the whole world. We must do all we can to revive, fortify, and strengthen our mann- Lactures, for it is in them our strength lies. We have a splendid inheritance. What is ,going to become of it We must cease to stand GY and watch the rich stream of raw material now by our doors; we must tap it at its source, and increase its value by our labours. As Sir A• Firth has said, "Means must be found to toake .it to the advantage of our Domini Ons to deal with the Mother Country, and to the -advantage of capitalists to embark on enter- prises within the King's Dominions in prefer- ence to investing their money in projects which 6e.,.,rve to strengthen potential enemies. Within 'lle British Dominions there is ample scope for enterprise in the investment of capital, and !Wile means must be found of encouraging to Lt,he utmost the development of the resources of "le Empire." As my space is now exhausted I must hold PVer any detailed statistics on raw materi:als for a future letter, merely clenching the argu- nle, I have advanced by a further quotation Lrotn Sir A. Firth; as follows:— We have hitherto preferred to act as inter- Inediary carrier, or clearing-house for foreign !lotions, making large profits out of handling ,the productions and financing the paper sym- uols which represent the productions of the 604 and factories of other nations. Often she never had any further-interest in those foreign productions beyond commissions earned by find- fig money to distribute them, for the foreign n,..ations that produced or consumed them, or tile carrying of them in our ships for profit. 't • ain's banking and dock sjrrtems thus be- rather international than national, with e inevitable result that she was content to Irglect her own national production so long as slne could earn money On the brokerage and the !.rrying of foreign productions. * PRAYER.
Viewed From Many Points By
Different Writers.

Concerning prayer, its nature, its difficulties and its value is a work of composite authorship which attempts to meet the difficulties of God's work in this present-day world, and the place and value of prayer. "God and the World's Pain," by the Rev. 8.. H. Streeter, regards God in his relation to life in the simile of an army. Ho is both directing general and non- commissioned officer. The general knows and is concerned with the whole scheme and plan of battle, but knows little .of the ,individual soldier. The non-commissioned officer is con- cerned only 'with the individual soldier, and knows nothing of the general plan of warfare. But God in human life knows and directs the whole plan, and is acquainted with the vicissitudes of the individual. The apparently abrupt close to a life may only evidence the long views of God. Christ closed his public ministry in three years. The Cross at the moment was the shame and the failure. The Cross became the throne of His glory. The momentary anguish of the individual will become his soul's salvation.

William F. Lofthouse, in his chapters upon "Prayer and The Old Testament," traces the evolution of Israel's emancipation from the con- ception of a tribal deity in which Jahveh stood in special relation to Israel as the God of vic- tory and prosperity; that Paganism tends to disappear, and is replaced by a devotion that is the spirit of all true religion. Writing upon "Prayer and Understanding," the Rev. H. Anson outlines the difference be- tween a Sultanic and scientific conception of God. The Sultanic concept libels God by pic- turing a deity who in one mood may be appeased, and in another mood cannot be approached. His wrath must cool before man can draw nigh. The scientific conception .of God is based upon "The Truth" or the Law of Nature. Nature cannot be tricked or cajoled. Nature is waiting to disclose her gifts to those ivho know how to approach her. With a scien- tific conception of prayer the suppliant knows that lack of response to his prayer is not be- cause the deity is angry, jiut because of 'the suppliant's disinclination to follow truth at Sill costs. The answer to prayer will come by an enlightenment of the mind, which opens out the laws of the kingdom. Acting upon such know- ledge the suppliant will continue to pray, conscious both of God's readiness to grant, and his own right as a son to pray, even though the request be delayed. The Boundaries of the Soul.

Dr. Rufus Jones continues the -argument in "Prayer and the Mystic Vision." No one, says he, can tell us the " esseutia " of prayer with- out revealing the level of their lives, and the. controlling influences and preferences of their lives. Heraclitus said "The boundaries of the soul cannot be discovered." There is another environment than that from which we draw our physical supplies. The sense of the indwelling spirit must be something more than a meta- physical conception. There 'Must be intimate personal experience. The actual content of religious faith are the slow accretions of racial experience, and do not come to us by the secret door of mystical openings. Yet the experience of the ripest souls is the communion of silence, and in that silence are impressive revelations of God.

Edward Bevan raises some real difficulties in his treatment of " Petition : Some Theoretical Difficulties." Is prayer necessary? If Ido not pray will God withhold any good? May not q man's good be otherwise than his desires? It might be better for a man to be ill than to be restored. His highest good may be in weak- ness. The relation of God to man as revealed in the New Testament is the relation of a father to a child. When that attitude is proven the utterance of a desire, the action in giving response may be sacramental. God may withhold the sought good and replace it by granting what is the true good. Supplication sweetens our relation to the Father. The second difficulty he raises is "Will God withhold good from anyone because I do not pray?" Is it thinkable that God would withhold any good to another simply because I failed to pray. It is undeniable that good in an individual, even as evil, reacts upon our fellow- men. My desire for a fellow man's good makes it possible for God to fulfil His love upon that man. God has willed that His love and His purpose should pass through human love. • How can one hear without a preacher? The necessity upon a believer to pray for the weal of his kind thus becomes a duty no 15e- Hever dare neglect. The third difficulty raised is "The insignificance of the individual." God has such a big world that He has no time to heed just one unit of the human race. The Rev. B. H. Streeter also deals with that phase and answers it.

Immanence. Rev. L. Hodgson, in his article on "Inter- cession," emphasises the suggestions of Edward Bevan. There is a, trinity in man as there is a trinity in God. God is immanent in all. The immanence in me is part of the immanence in my neighbour. The repeated intercession of my soul to God must therefore affect the soul of my neighbour.

A. C. Turner geems to regard the value and efficacy of prayer to consist in the mystical growth of conviction within. A faith which in its expression tends to make actual that in which it believes. To pray for the setting in motion of unseen forces to compel your will upon men (or as you deem God's will) however excel- lent your object may be, is distinctly wrong. "To attempt to think of spiritual efficacy In terms of outward relations of cause and effect will land you in the neighbourhood of magic." There are, says Turner, "No spiritual dynamics." The expression of such views evidently puts his position differently than other writers in the book.

The other articles of the book are equally stimulating and suggestive. As the Editor says, men are asking "Has prayer an active. value? Should it not safely be left to ministers, monks and pious ladies who have nothing else to do?" The mind that is anxious t 6 know how .prayer may be applied in the present day will find in the volume under review an honest attempt to deal with the situation. Around a table these men and women have conferred. Their views have no uniformity. Indeed there are very divergent views, even opposed views, but a thinker must find that which meets his spiritual need. H. O.

Mr. B. Seebohm Powntree, the noted socioiogist and ideal employer, here contributes the first of two interesting articles upon a them 3 which is especially vital in these days.

Some employers tell you they do not know what welfare supervision means. This is only because it is a new name for something which has been carried on to a greater or lesser ex- tent ever since there were factories. Welfare supervision is simply the creation In a factory of those conditions which enable each indivi- dual worker to be and to do his or her best.

So long as factories were very small th4re was no need of any special organisation to securo this end; the 'master knew each of his men personally, and if he were wise he saw that each was put to the work best fitted for him, and worked under thoroughly good con- ditions which enabled him to do his hest both for himself, and his employer. But as factories grew larger and larger this personal -relation was crowded out. The employer no longer knew his workers even by name. They came to be impersonal "factory hands" to him, who were treated in the mass, without individual con- sideration. Even when he honestly desired to do well by them, • it was increasingly difficult for any worker who had some personal griev- ance to get it remedied, and too little care was taken to suit the work to the worker, and sur- round him with conditions tending to efficiency. Gradually it became clear that this state of things was unsatisfactory from every point of view, and many eniployers appointed special officers simply to re-establish the personal re- lation between themselves and the workers, which still exists in many small factories. The special officers undertaking this work bear dif- ferent names in different factories; but perhaps the most usual title is that of "Welfare Super- visor," which was adopted by the Health of Munition Workers' Committee when writing on the subject in relation to munitions fac- tories. Both men and women welfare super- visors have been appointed, though the latter greatly outnumber the former, and it is of welfare supervision among women that the Editor has more especially asked me to write.

div.head: Not A Fad.
div.p: Not A Fad.

Some employers may think that welfare supervision is merely a fad. This is quite a mistaken view. It is not only good from the workers' standpoint, rendering life in the factory more comfortable, healthy and happy, but it is thoroughly Sound business from the standpoint of the employer. As a matter of fact, it is stupid to treat workers in the mass, and only through lack of insight do we fail to realise its stupidity.

For it nlust be remembered that a manu- facturer's equipment is of two kinds----human and mechanical. What should we think of an employer who treated his machinery in the mass? As a matter of fact, he watches his mechanical equipment with extraordinary care. It is continually tested to find if there is any overstrain. A man goes round with an oil-can ml day long to see that there is no unnecessary friction anywhere. Peripdical inspections of the plant are made. Andefinally you have the engineer doinc, nothing else but seeing after the welfare of the machines. It is recognised, in a .word, that each machine iiaust be dealt with separately. Now human beings are infinitely more com- plex and more delicate than machines. Not- withstanding this "hands" are faken on with but scant consideration of the particular work for which they are best suited, and little effort is made to interest them in what they are going to do, or to create in them a desire to succeed. A sensitive girl may be engaged by a rough-tempered foreman and put to work without a word of encouragement in a great room full of strangers under the supervision of a nagging overlooker. ' Although she may never have been in a factory before she is 'expected to work a twelve-hour shift, sometimes in a very bad atmosphere, and often but scanty provision is made to enable her to get a good meal in the middle of the day, amid comfortable and rest- ful surroundings. Need we wonder at it if her work is inefficient. A girl will never do the best for her employer or for herself under such conditions.

If only employers would treat their employes with as much consideration as they do their machines they would have less difficulty in getting satisfactory output, and the workers would be spared much ill-health and suffering. 48 Hours Long Enough.

Some specific questions about every-day diffi- culties have been put to me. I will answer them as best I may. First of all, how long can women work effi- ciently? It is impossible to lay down any hard and fast rule as to the number of hours girls can work with advantage. It depends upon the severity of the labour, the conditions under which the worker k live at home, the transit difficulties, the atmospheric conditions in the factory, and the wages paid. But, broadly speaking, I think that the demand of the workers for a 48 hours' week is based upon reason. The advantage of going below it is doubtful, and I am pretty sure that, as a rule, there is little, if any, use in going much above it, except for short periods. Generally speak- ing, then, I should say the employer is wise who works his women and girls for $i hours per day from Monday to Friday, and for five hours on Saturday. I question whether it over pays to keep on working girls for more than 54 hours a week. As for the 60 hours' week, it is most unsatisfactory. A short break of, say, ten minutes in the middle of the morning is a distinct advantage. There is much evidence to show how great a relief it is to the workers, many of whom COMO away from home with no breakfast, or an in- adequate one, and are thus enabled to get a little lunch. In some munition factories milk is being sold to the workers during this break, and is an excellent plan. In many they are allowed to go to the canteen for tea or other refreshments. I am asked whether it is desirable for women to work at night. Certainly not; but if for any reason (as, for instance, the exigencies of war-time) it is absolutely necessary, then it is far better to work women on three shifts of eight hours than to work two shifts of twelve hours.

next comes the question of canteens. Are they worth while? The Americans recognise rinich more fully than we do the advantages of giiod canteen arrangements in the works. We have all heard that "a man can be neither a statesman, a philosopher, a poet, nor a lover unless he has had something to eat during the last 48 hours." This is doubtless true, but it is just as true that unless girls in a factory can get a comfortable mid-day meal they can- not be expected to do a good afternoon's work. I have heard employers speak of comfortable mess-rooftts as luxuries and fads, and of a good canteen as involving a capital expenditure which brings in no return. The Goose and Gander.

Nothing is further from the truth. Employ- em know perfectly well that if they themselves lunch hurriedly on badly-cooked and unnutri- tious food their work suffers, and what is true of them is true of their workers. If they are to do a good afternoon's work they need a restful dinner hour and nutritious food. There is some truth in a remark I once heard that "left to herself a woman always tends to live pon cake," and this is a danger which should be guarded against in the canteens.

Another of the general conditions which a wise employer will carry out in his factory -is to See that the ventilation of his workrooms is good, that they are adequately warmed, that the air is fresh, and that they are well lighted. We are quite alive to the importance of these things in our own offices. ..When the air is stuffy we find that our brains are sluggish, and we open the window. If we are too cold or too hot, and if the sun is shining in our eyes, or the artificial lights are too strong or too weak, we remedy the 'defect, because it inter- feres with our work.

Yet we wander through our workrooms, see- ing such defects multiplied indefinitely, ana wholly fail to realise that the workers are just as sensitive as we are, and that it is extremely had business to handicap them by irritating conditions. Indeed, we grumble at the Home Office Inspectors and call them faddists, be- cause they fluid upon a certain minimum in the way of ventilation and lighting 1

This Season's Parasols.

Parasols are of great diversity, never more so, nor have they ever been more charming. For those who take a seaside holiday, there are useful and gaily flowered chintz, cretonne, and tussore sunshades, the latter lined with some delicate colour repeated in the holiday frock. The handles are in porcelain and as dainty as the parasols themselves. But the real Japanese umbrella will lead the van, at the seaside at any rate; it has already scored a triumph, and its career has only just commenced. Certainly the charge of monotony cannot be brought against designers ,of parasols, who have rung every possible change on the shapes to which we have been so long accustomed. The newest black and white sunshades look like big Chinese lanterns; when shut one half is black, the other white, the latter forming the inside when open. The tiny Victorian parasol is re- served for carriage wear in the park, and pro- vides sufficient shade for the eyes without hid- ing any part of a beautiful toilette. Salt and Starch.

Baker's brown bread is generally very salt, and often the white is, too, and that is why it is better to make the bread at home when pos- sible. With some people, if they take much salt, it causes irritation of the skit, and others .have had dandruff and dryness of the hair—a good point to urge in advising against the use of salt in preparing food for young children. One of the most ordinary forms of dyspepsia is due to undigested starch remaining in the stomach and causing an excessive secretion of hydrochloric acid. As long as proteid food is present the pepsin and acid expend themselves on it, and are removed together, but the un- digested starch continues to set up gastric secretion, an 4 the remaining acrid causes pain and heartbuni and flatulence. This will be in- creased if there is any butyric acid in the food or any other fatty acid derived from milk, butter, or cheese. There are several methods of treating this fowl of indigestion. First of all, all starchy foods must be cooked thoroughly, and the eating of starch in the form of 'hard and dry biscuits, crusts, and other hard foods, which need thorough mastication and moisten- ing with saliva, should be encouraged. This necessitates the keeping of the food for some time in the mouth.

Women and Inorganic Chemistry. The girl student, in search of a career, could not do better than turn her attention to dyes and their allied branches of 'research work, which will afford her an opportunity of turn- ing her knowledge to profitable account. So far women have not been greatly'attracted in the direction of inorganic chemistry; possibly because before the war there was no opening for them, the positions in factories and other places being invariably filled, by highly-trained Germans. The war, however, has altered this condition of things, and as the colour sense is more highly developed in women than in men, research work in dyes should appeal specially to them. The work too is most interesting. The Germans fully realised the importance of fast and beautiful colours in dress materials, and where we had a hundred chemists they had a thousand. Now that the School of Technology at Manchester has established a sub department for research work in regard to dyes, there is reason to hope that we may not only supply our own demands, but obtain some of Ger- many's trade as well.

Niece Edna Fellows, 44, Bewsey-road (Evelyn- street School), sends a very fine account of a ramble through Arley Woods, near Higher Ince, Wigan. "We came to a farmhouse," she says, "which I could see was very, very old, for it seemed as though it had once been a castle; the battlements were still standing, and also two turrets. Here we got tea, which we drank to some lunch that we nad brought with us, while sitting in a big field opposite the farm. Afterwards we went- into the depths of the woods. It was so lovely and quiet, not a sound, except the singing of the birds, the rustling of the wind amongst the leaves of the trees, and the peaceful rippling of the rivOr Douglas as it flowed through the valley in the woods. We passed over the river Douglas by a small wooden bridge. On the, opposite side of the river the ground sloped gently upwards, and on the slope all kinds of flowers were grow- ing. There were buttercups, daisies, lesser celandines and lots of other flowers. We climbed to the top of the hill and then looked round about. On one side of us was the valley, Lill of trees and flowers, and the river flowing merrily along. On another side were some fields, and rising up above them were the moun- tains. div.head: HOUSES NEEDED.
div.p: HOUSES NEEDED.
Trades Council Writes To The
Ministry Of Munitions.
"KEYS FOR AUCTION."

At their meeting on Tuesday evening the Warrington Trades and Labour Council had again under discussion the question of housing accommodation, which is of such vital import- ance to the workers and residents generally.

The C 04,1161 had communicated with the Ministry of Munitions on the subject, and a reply had been received stating that the case did not appear to be one in which the Minister of Munitions could take any action, the duty of meeting the housing requirements of Warring- ton being one which rests with the local authority. The Chairman (Mr. Edwin Plinston) : And the local authority is the Town Council. Alder- man James Evans said that something is going to be done, but we have got to wait and see. We have pinned the proper authority at all events. The responsibility is entirely with the Town Council.

One of the delegates remarked that he thought those who took down houses were bound to re- place them. They should build before they began to pull down. Mr. Charles Dukes (secretary) said that if a railway company were. going to clear anybody out in order to make extensions they had to make provision for them. That obligation did riot, however, apply to !other owners of pro- perty, who were also employers of labour. If they required to extend their property and they wanted the land Upon which the houses stood, it was purely a business transaction. Like other landlords, they gave their tenants notice to flit. It was some three or four years ago since a deputation was appointed to meet the Town Council. Alderman James Evans was on that committee, and it was stated from their point of view that the time was then opportune for the provision of housing accommodation for the workmen, but they got "no forrarder." At that time he (Mr. Dukes) stated that there was concerted action on the part of the builders not to erect cottage property with a view to creat- ing a scarcity of houses, and so inflating the rents. The builders had proved themselves good business men, and had succeeded in their object. The idea of municipal dwellings en- joyed by -members of the Town Council was something in the nature of what they could see in Salford and Liverpool, and which, to him, was nothing but a human rookery. (Hear, hear.) That was not the solution of the housing problem at all. Some years ago a progressive Town Council would have built dwellings which were sorely needed then. To erect cottage pro- perty now, at the price of material, would in- evitably result in a rent higher than what was being paid at present for much of the insanitary property in the locality. Agents of landlords were going about putting up keys for auction, and scores of people had their, names down as prospective tenants for one house, yet men still argued that there was no housing problem. There had been a housing problem in Warrington for years, but until the personnel of the Town Council was altered he had no confidence that the question would be properly tackled. Mr. Hamblett suggested that they should write the Town Clerk calling attention to the matter, and the meeting so decided.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE.
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE.
Fibre Works Gutted And R.C. Schools Have Narrow Escape.

Through a fire which occurred on Sunday night, the bristle, bass and fibre works of Messrs. Thomas Rushworth and Sons, Ltd., in Clegg-street,. off Orford-line, were completely wrecked and damage extending to several thousands of pounds was done. St. Benedict's Roman Catholic Schools, which adjoin, had an exceedingly narrow but successful escape from destruction, thanks to the efforts of the fire brigade, under the supervision of Superin- tendent Frank Turner.

The brigade received a telephone message shortly after eight o'clock and proceeded to the scene with the motor engine.. On arrival thy found that the works-50 yards toy 21.1—was on fire from end to end, and it was obvious that there was little hope of saving either the structure or the inflammable material inside. The many tons of fibre were crackling up. roariously. Fortunately, there was no wind, or else the efforts of the brigade in preventing the fire spreading to the adjoining property would have been even more difficult of achieve- ment.

A large crowd assembled, and Inspector Stuart and a posse of police (including special constables) kept them at a safe distance. Hundreds of them stayed until well past mid- night. After six hours' hard labour by the brigade the fire was got under control, and the motor engine was free to be sent home, but half a dozen jets, attached to hydranvs, had to be used until nine 'o'clock in the morning before it was safe to leave the scene.
Apart from one end of it, the works was completely wrecked.

The Warrington Board of Guardians wrote to the Runcorn Guardians on Tuesday asking for authority to pay out-relief amounting to Bs. 6d. instead of ss. to a woman who lives in Warrington, and is chargeable to the Runcorn Union. The Acting Clerk (Mr. W. E. Hough) explained that some time ago the Runcorn Guardians refused to increase the relief in this case.

Mr: Antwis : This is the case the Warrington Guardians had so much to say about. Mr. Ho.ugh stated that the woman was 66 years of age, and was living apart from her husband. The rent of her house was 6s. 6d.
Mr. Linaker, sen.: She cannot live as cheaply in a town like Warrington as in the country. I think it is a case where we might give an in- crease.
Mr. Spruce: But 6s. 6d. is a high figure for rent. The suggested increase seems to be out- rageous.

For some time, the Clerk said, the woman had been in receipt of ss. per week out-relief, which was paid by Warrington on behalf of Runcorn. She was paying 6s. Gs. per week rent, earning 3s. a week by plain sewing, and receiving 12s. a week from a son. The son left home, and in December of last year the Warrington Board asked that the relief be increased to 10s. a week. If the case were in their own Union would they give any relief at all? A Member: If she cannot pay a rent of 6s. 6d. she should live in a smaller house.

The Clerk went on to say that the husband was now receiving the old age pension. He understood that a gentleman who conducted certain inquiries on behalf or Warrington told him that unless he sent ss. per week towards his wife's maintenance there wouvt be trouble. Mr. Pilling: He did pay 3s. 6d. a week at first. Alderman Norman : What should we do if was in our own Union?

The Chairman: We shouldn't be so generous. The Clerk: The case was dealt with in 1913, and the Board dia not then think it was a case fot out-relief, but on the strong representation of Warrington they agreed to pay out-relief. The husband is now ill and is in lodgings in Widnes. Mr. Hallows moved that the woman be offered the house.
The Chairman: That is rather going too far. We seem wedded to ss.
The Clerk: Warrington have paid 3s. 6d. a week extra for some weeks.
It was agreed that the Warrington Board's request for increased relief be not acceded to.

div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY AUGUST 12, 1916.
BRITISH-NOT GERMAN- EDUCATION.

The resignation of fr. HENDERSON from the position of the President of the Board of Education is taken as the sign direct that the Government are about to undertake in earnest the reform of our educa- tional system. Mr. HENDERSON is rendering; valuable service to the Government in ad- vising them in Labour matters—an occupa- tion that is second to none in importance now that we are 'relying upon the workers of the country to blast the enemy out of the terri- tories of our Allies. That advice will still be at the disposal of the Government. But education relates to the future; and it re- quires the urgent undivided attention of a whole-time man. A suggestion has been made that the man to be appointed should be one who has had practical experience of teaching; but it may be doubted whether a genius could be found who ,would combine practical experience and the organising ability that the educational reformer would require for the gigantic task that lies before him. Yesterday the "Daily Chronicle" stated that the official announcement of LORD CREWE'S appointment as Minister of Educa- tion will be made at an early date. LORD

CREWE has had great experience of an all- round character, in which the welfare of the child, mentally and physically, has had a large place, and it would be difficult to find a better occupant for the vacant post; but the personal element is not, for the moment, a matter about which we need to have very deep concern. The occasion will produce the man.

What we, the people of the country, have to make sure about is that the occasion itself is produced. We must see that our educa- tional system is thoroughly overhauled and brought into line. with 'what we know will assuredly be the conditions when the war has been brought to a close. We shall beat Ger- many in the field; we must make such pro- vision that we shall as surely beat her in commerce when the war is over. We do not want to ape Germad methods; in the main we must abhor them. But there are lessons to be learnt and to be benefited from, if they are German lessons, and of -these we shall no doubt take rational advantage. Let it be clearly understood, however, that we are not going to Germanise our schools any more than we are going to Germanise our institu- tions or our morals. Of course, if we so de- graded our schools, the other degradations would follow, because our children are the foundation upon which, for good or for evil, we build for all time. Those who are calling for German methods of " efficiency" in this direction or the other, would do well to pon- der over the real meaning of what they de- mand. SIR JAMES YOXALL recently told us. " So far," .said this practical expert, " as. I have been able to understand, the German professors and teachers taught patriotism as though it were an arrogant bombast; they taught language and literature is though it were a science; they taught science as though it were a trade, and they taught trade as though trading meant swindling:. Any pro- posal to import ideals or methods of that kind into this country is one which, I think, every earnest patriot here ought strongly to condemn." We do condemn it and do not intend to see it set up over our own system, which has produced character in our man- hood that is shining throughout the world to-day in great and enviable contrast to the miserable kultur that the German system has produced. What we have to do is to take our own system and improve it; and having improved it, to see that our children get the best re- sults from it. For instance, we cannot beat a swindling nation when of our 2,750,00 u school children between twelve and sixteen years of age only 1,100,000 remain in our schools beyond the age of 13. We cannot beat the Germans if, in a town like Warring- ton, a hundred scholars who do desire to con- tinue a higher educational course are turned adrift in one year for lack of places for them in the Secondary School. What we require is commonsense applied to our own system; then we could well afford to let the Germans and their soul-killing systems stay in the country where they appear to find such con- genial soil as would be hard to discover on this side of the North Sea.

div.head: DOMINION TEA PARTY.
div.p: DOMINION TEA PARTY.
Wounded Australians And Canadians Entertained.

• Moving out of the Bold-street soldiers' re- creation rooms through a side-door into the beautiful garden at the rear of the home of the Rev. and Mrs. E. C. E. Carleton, between fifty and sixty wounded Colonials were entertained to tea on Thursday. Their nurses were to have been with them, but ,the arrival- of another convoy at the Lord Derby Hospital prevented their coming. Most of the men hailed from Australia, seven or eight being from Canada, but they ate things with the same heartiness as our own ," Tom- plies." It was a rare tea. div.head: WARRINGTON SUMMER CAMP.
div.p: WARRINGTON SUMMER CAMP.
Nearly 150 Boys Enjoy A Week At
Prestat)m.

The first batch of boys arrived t the Summer Camp at Prestatyn on Saturday. The boys, 144 in number, were under the charge of Mr. Hol- brook (superintendent) and Messrs. Groake, Greenhough, Hammond, Oxley, Turner and Weir. Saturday afternoon was spent on the shore, many boys for the first time in their lives, having a view of the ocean. The first night, as usual, was rather a ..estless one for the children, as they had not settled down to camp beds and huts.
Sunday was spent in a very quiet manner. A short walk was taken over the Golf Links, and the remainder of the day was spent upon the shore.

By the time Monday had arrived the children had thoroughly settled down and had made their minds up to spend a glorious week. Rhyl was visited in the morning; the "bank" was opened, and the boys visited the various shops on the Promenade. Monday afternoon the boys were taken in the sea, which was thoroughly enjoyed. Many visitors cm the shore stated they had never seen such a sight-140 boys all stripped waiting for the whistle to blow signalling them to run across the stretch of sands and dive in the sea. At the word of command the sands seemed to be alive. The person who missed a glorious chance was the cinematograph operator. Tuesday morning, the boys were, taken to Presfatyn beach, which was crowded with visitors. Many of the boys, born humorists, seemed to entertain the crowd better than the pierrots. Wednesday was a "red letter day." The boys were taken to Rhyl to spend the whole day. A start was made at 9.30 a.m., and camp was reached again at 6 p.m. The Rhyl Marine Lake was the principal place visited, the manager generously allowing the children to take part in the various amusements at half the usual prices. Sandwiches and lemonade were taken from the camp in a huge hamper by train. The children all sat down by the Marine Lake to eat their dinner. Coming home the boys walked along the Rhyl Promenade, so the whole of Rhyl front was seen by all. _ _

Thursday was sports day. Many splendid prizes were got together, and the events were run off in grand style. There were flat races, three-legged races, long distance races, &c. Friday, the returning day, was spent in Pres-

tatyn. the boys visiting the various shops to take home presents of every description. War- rington was reached last evening at 9.30, the tanned faces of the boys showing that a glorious week had been spent by the seaside. Every credit is due to the cooks, Mr. and Mrs. Fulton, who have studied the children in every detail, preparing dishes that exactly suited them.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AUL HERBERT PLUMPTON.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AUL HERBERT PLUMPTON.

On Tuesday afternoon the remains of the late Mr. Herbert Plumpton, managing director of the firm of Messrs. Herbert Plumpton, Ltd., engineers and tool manufacturers, Liverpool- road, were interred in Daresbury Churchyard. The Rev. T. T. Lee-Jopes officiated. The principal mourners were Messrs. Thomas Plumpton (son), George Plumpton and Frank Plumpton (brothers), George Harding, Samuel Plumpton, Stephen Plumpton and Cyril Plump- ton (nephews), E. A. Bradbury (cousin), H. Hal- ford, J. Harding and F. Atkinson (brothers-in- law), William Summerfield and Samuel Sum- merfield (uncles), and Messrs. W. Clatworthy and J. Cannon. A number of employes of the firm acted as bearers. Floral tributes were sent by the following "His loving wife and children," "Brother George and Nephew Sam," "His loving brother Frank, Tom and Kitty," Mr. and Mrs. Clat- worthy, Mr. and Mrs. E. A. Bradbury and Miss Gladys Bradbury, Mr. and Mrs. Woodward, "Auntie Jeannie, Stevie, Molly and Cyril," Mr. and Mrs. A. de Prez and family, Mr. and Mrs. S. Summerfield, and the employes of the firm.' The late Mr Plumpton died at his residence, Sandhurst, Moore, on Saturday, from heart trouble, which became very pronounced after the death of his brother, Mr. Stephen Plump- ton, who passed away so recently as May 16th. He was the eldest son of the late Councillor George Plumpton, and leaves a widow, one son and two daughters. He was the founder of the firm already mentioned and under his guidance during the past twenty years the business was extremely successful. He was for many years a member of Wycliffe Congregataonal Church, Warrington, but latterly worshipped at the Wesleyan Church, Moore. His principal hobby was gardening and he was a successful grower of many choice flowers.

div.head: BIGGEST PARADE.
div.p: THE BIGGEST PARADE.
Conditionally Exempted Men
With The Volunteers.
COMMANDANT RYLANDS'S ENCOURAGEMENT.

The obligation now placed by Military Tri- bunals on men conditionally exempted from active service is beginning to bear fruit, and the first parade of new members of the Warrington Company V.T.C. was very gratifying from the point of numbers. Officers, non-commissioned officers and men on parade totalled 23L Of these about 50 were former members, and formed the first platoon. Postcards announcing the time and place of 'meeting (Drill Hall, 7.30), had been sent to each man, and although many recipients were prob- ably unavoidably absent, the response was con- sidered satisfactory by Commandant W. P. Rylands. Th% men assembled fairly punctually and, with few exceptions, appeared to be well under thirty years of age, so that the drill officers will have plenty of good material to work upon. It goes without saying that Warrington should turn out a fine _serviceable battalion that would bring credit on the town. The majority of men on parade settled down very quickly to their surroundings, and no doubt those who were somewhat lax and chafed a little at the enforced restraint- will soon have the corners knocked off and gain enthusiasm as the work progresses. Acting Adjutant W. Ashton and the section officers formed' the men into squads according to name initials, and they were marked off on the -roll.
Proficiency To Be Attained.
The parade having been called to attention,

Commandant RylaTnds made an encouraging speech and appealed to the men to give as much time as they could to drilling. He knew, course, how long many of them ,were engaged at their work, but it was remarkable ho W little time it took to make a man proficient. He urged upon them to make some sacrifice at home in order to help in every way they could the men who were making so many sacrifices for 115 in France. He pointed out • how useful the Volunteer force could be, and although invasion was very unlikely after our Jutland victory, we should all he prepared. They should also be able to turn out well when they were welcom- ing the return Of our victorious troops. \He mentioned that the ceremony of enrolment and taking: the oath of allegiance would take place the following Sunday (to-morrow) at the Town Hall at 11 o'clock, and also asked them to endeavour to attend the parade service arranged for the 20th inst. It was proposed to have drills each night in the Drill Hall at eight o'clock, and they had a number of most efficient instruc- tors.

Acting-Adjutant Ashton called for volunteers to help on Navy Day next Thursday. They would he principally required to act as stewards in Bank Park, and he would want 40 men- in the afternoon and 80 at nieht. The first party would take. up duty at 1.30 and the second at 6.30.

There .was a good response to Mr. Ashton's appeal. The parade then formed fours and marched for a short way through the town by Sankey- street, Bridge-street, Rvlands-street and Bold- street to the Town Hall, where they were dis- missed.
The officers present were Commandant Rylands, Acting-Adjutant W. Ashton, Platoon- Commander Mathias, Company-Sergeant-Major Sullivan and Sergeant-Instructor Delooze.

div.head: Mr. F. A. Frost Warns Some
div.p: Mr. F. A. Frost Warns Some
Exempted Men.

Mr. F. A. Frost, who is a member of the Warrington Recruiting Tribunal, visited the Star Kinema House on Monday evening, and after witnessing an exhibition of a number of films showing an inspection of Volunteers in London, by the late Lord Kitchener, was granted permission to make a reeruiting'speech on behalf of the Volunteer Training Corps in this district. - -

During his speech Mr. Frost said he Evould like to give a word of warning—not a threat, but a little friendly advice—to a number of men, who had been before the Tribunal and obtained conditional exemptio;r, one condition being that they should join the' Volunteers and become efficient. "I heard it said that that is a very easy condition to fulfil, that men can join a Volunteer Corps and shortly afterwards send in 14 days' notice, and thus fulfil the con- dition they had agreed to," he added. "I am a member of the Warrington Military Tribunal. and I can say that that won't do. I am. of emirse, speaking for myself, but can fuy tint the condition is there, and that if it is not carried out when a man's case again comes before the Tribunal, the fact of his resignation would weigh very heavily With me. Possibly the exemption would be cancelled, and the man would be drafted as a private in the Army straight away. I don't use any threat; this is friendly advice. Mr. Frost regarded it as being the duty of all men who could to do their bit, and he con- sidered that Warrington should have, at least, two full battalions of Volunteers. In conclu- sion, Mr. Frost expressed his gratitude to the management of the Star Kinema House for permitting him to make a speech.

Curious trifling with a special constable who challenged him for riding a bicycle without a front light and red rear-light, was mentioned to the Borough magistrates on Friday, when John William Bower, butcher, Buttermarket- street, was fined 11}3. in each ease.
