div.head: IN GREAT ADVANCE.
div.p: IN GREAT ADVANCE.
Captain Sydney T. Boast, of the South Lanca- shire Regiment, writing on August sth to Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk of Warrington, says

- "The• cigarettes mentioned in your letter of 14th July arrived safely yesterday, and were duly distributed last night. The tobacco arrived a few days ago and was also distributed. The smokes were very .welcome and much appreciated by the men, on whpse behalf I ask you to con- vey to the subscribers to your fund very sincere thanks. We are all very grateful for your kind thoughts in sending these very acceptable gifts of smokes.
"Since I last wrote to' you the Battalion has done some very severe fighting, and although our casualties were heavy, it is satisfactory to kndw that all ranks did splendidly.

div.head: FOUGHT SPLENDIDLY AGAINST ENEMY'S FINEST TROOPS.
div.p: FOUGHT SPLENDIDLY AGAINST ENEMY'S FINEST TROOPS.

"On 3rd July our 'Brigade took part in the attack on disposition of the enemy's machine guns the main object was not obtained. During the evening of the 3rd July the Brigade was withdrawn to support (the line being taken over by fresh troops) and. remained in this position until the afternoon of the 7th, when the Brigade moved into the vicinity of . on the following morning the Battalion moved forward and took part in the operations in con- nection with the attack on . Later the Battalion again withdrew to support and re- mained in this position until the night of 11th, ,when it again moved forward in relW .of another Battalion of the Brigade. Eventually the Battalion took part in the actual attack on , and obtained a footing in the outskirts the village, the .enemy, • Prussian Guards, making most determined efforts to .prevent a lodgment of our men. On following days fur- ther advances and expanses were made, more ground was gained and consolidated. Our losses were again heavy, but those of the crpray were greater. Our men fought splendidly. A number of prisoners were taken and two machine guns captured. Throughout the whole of the operations every Battalion of the Diviion to Which we belong took part, and . a stubborn' defence was offered with determination and courage by some of the enemy's finest troons. Many acts of gallantry were performed by many of our officers and men. Some rewards have already been made, and it is hoped there are more to tome.
COMMANDER'S CONGRATULATIONS.

"On the 16th July the Battalion with other units of our, Brigade, was withdrawn after nearly a fortnight's hard fighting, and in a Special order of the day' issued on the 17th July, our Corps Commander expressed to the G.O.C.- and all ranks of our Division his appreciation of their gallantry and devotion to duty, and congratulated them, on. the final success of their efforts in . After a few days' rest, during which opportunity was taken to re-fit the Battalion and obtain. reinforce- ments, the Battalion returned to another sector of the line which we now hold. From this you will see we have lately had a very busy time, and our men have worked hard. On withdrawal from the line on 16th July everyone was very tired, but even aftergonly a few hours' rest it was surprising how soon they forgot their troubles and how cheerful everyone was. As already explained, we have sustained a con- siderable number of casualties, but even up to now, quite a number of men who were only slightly wounded have rejoined, and in spite of their recent experiences, they are all eager to 'resume business.' Lately the weather has been very hot and trying.

div.head: COLONEL COTTON, C.O.
div.p: COLONEL COTTON, C.O.

"Our Commanding Officer, Colonel Cotton, who was recently awarded the D. 5.0., and who has many friends in Warrington and district, is still with us, a fact for which we are all very thankful and fortunate, considering the severity of the fighting and the recent experiences. Several Battalions unfortunately lost their Commanding Officers. It may be of general in- terest to know that our Battalion, which is one of the units .of our Brigade, took part in all the operations mentioned, in conjunction with ourselves, and did excellent work. Un- fortunately on the last day, just before our withdrawal from the situation, Colonel Brassev, commanding that Battalion, was killed. He was a • most popular and efficient officer, and his loss was very much felt by all ranks in his and our own Battalion."

Numerous Successes By Our

Following the report which appeared in our last week's issue of the regimental spbrts of the Territorial Reserve Battalion, Warrington people will be glad to hear that representatives of the local battalion competed very success- fully in the athletic sports held in connection with the garrison of which the 4th South Lancashires form a part. div.p: MUTINY VETERAN.
Peter Dennett Dies Suddenly In His Eightieth Year.

Another of Warrington's veterans has passed away in the person of Mr. Peter Dennett, of 138, Knutsford-road, whose death took place suddenly on Wednesday. The late Mr. Dennett, who was 79 years of age, served in the Indian Mutiny with the Madras Fusiliers (East Indian Company) and was the proud possessor of the medal and bar. div.head: CRIMEAN VETERAN.
div.p: CRIMEAN VETERAN.
Private Patrick Miskell Buried
With Military Honours.

When Private Patrick Niskell, late of Her Majesty's Royal Berkshire Regiment of foot— because he shouldered his musket in the spacious days of Queen Victoria—fought in the Crimea, he little dreamt of the circumstances which would attend his funeral in Warrington sixty-two years later. Private Miskell was an Irishman, and having lived in Warrington for some years, resided latterly at Dam-lane, Rixton. He was well over 80 years of age, 85 in fact, and after the death of. his wife lived a lonely life. He became seriously ill eight or ten weeks ago, and was removed for suitable treatment and nursing to Whitecross Hospital. He died on Wednesday. In the Mayoralty of Alderman Smethurst a Veterans' Committee was formed, having as hon. treasurer Mr. John Fairhurst, borough treasurer. Its object was a very laudable one. Knowing the financial difficulties into which old soldiers were sometimes plunged—Army pen- sioners being paid quarterly—it was suggested that the men, by assigning their pensions to the Borough Treasurer, could get the amount in weekly instalments. The privilege was eagerly availed of—especially as the weekly 'payment was augmented from a sum raised by subscrip- tion. Private Miskell *as the last of these beneficiaries, and it was regretted that the effort of the committee some three months ago to get him into Chelsea Hospital did not suc- ceed: As far as the committee knew, the veteran had no relatives. He was alway§ cheery when calling at the Borough Treasurer's office for his weekly dole. He chatted of old times; of weary nights by the bank of the Tchernaya River— waiting for the Russians—and then speaking of the present war, wished that he could have had a "cut in" this time.

The funeral took place at 1.30 yesterday, and was attended by Aldermftn Smethurst and Alderman Bennett, with' the Borough Treasurer as representing the Veteran's Committee. The coffin was conveyed in a hearse and covered with the Union Jack, pall bearers 'being supplied by the Depot* of the South Lancs. Regiment. It was preceded by a firing party supplied by the Warrington Company V.T.C., composed of a corporal and twelve men, in charge of Sergt. W. 'Ashton. There was also a bugler. They marched with rifles reversed through the streets of the town out Cemetery way, where a 'bus conveyed them the rest of the route to Woolston,' where the interment took place in the graveyard adjoining the Roman Catholic Church. When the remains were laid in the grave three volleys were fired, the "Last Post" was sounded and the Crimean N;eteran was left to rest in peace.

Chaplain's Opinion of Col. Crosfield. The Rev. F. G. Goddard, a returned chaplain from the Front, has made a point of dissemin- ating news of men on active se' vice among their friends at home. The fete was held in the grounds around the hospital, and, the day being gloriously fine, people flocked in their hundreds to the scene of gaiety. Tea was served on the lawn at a moderate charge, and here " Tommy " was again to be seen wielding the tray like an expert waiter. The tit-bits of the day, however, were the concerts, the rendezvous of which was a marquee pitched in the centre of the grounds. Crowded "houses" were the order at both per- formances, one in the afternoon and another in the evening, and everyone expressed himself and herself as being delighted with the displays given. This is all the More creditable in view of the facts that the concert had been organised by two patients at the hospital, Lance-Ccirporal Kerrigan and Rifleman Batty, and that the troupe consisted entirely of nurses and patients from the hospital, who had been trained to- gether only for a short time. Stoios.—Put from 4oz. to 6oz. of fresh oat- meal, ground as fine as flour, into a pan, .mix with a little cold water to the substance of cream, then add soz. or 6oz. of loaf sugar, and a fresU lemon cut in thin slices, with .the pips taken out. Add a gallon of boiling water. Stir thoroughly while the water is being poured on. Use hot, warm, or cold. The lemon may be omitted, or any other flavouring used in: istead. Four lemons are enough for five gallons.

Cokos is a good nourishing drink, made as follows :—Four oz. of fresh fine ground oatmeal, 2 to 4oz. of cocoa, into a pan mixed with a little cold water into a thin batter, then add 6oz. sugar, pour on a gallon of boiling water (stir while 'water is being added); take to the field in stone jar.

Hopkos is a good harvest drink.—Boil loz. of hops and ioz. of ginger (bruised) in 11 gallons of water for 25 minutes; add 11b. of best brown sugar, and boil ten minutes more, then strain, and bottle or put into a cask while hot; it will be ready for drinking when cold. It should be kept in a cold place. Dried hore- hound may be used instead of hops. Com- pressed English hops may be obtained in 11b. packets from grocers and chemists. No yeast must be used in making hopkos. Lemonade.-1. For present use.—Put 11b. of white sugar, loz. cream of tartar, and two lemons, cut in slices (or a teaspoonful of essence of lemon), in a large jug, and pour over all 3 quarts of boiling water. This is a very cooling drink. 2. For bottling.—Dissolve 21b. of lump sugar in a quart of boiling water, add 2oz. of citric acid, and two lemons sliced (or e teaspoonful of essence of lemon); stir together, strain, and bottle when cold. A tablespoonful, more of less, in a glass of water will make a pleasant drink. Note.—One lemon is about equal to 10 drops of essence of lemon, or to A drachm of citric acid. If essence of lemon is used in place of lemon it should be mixed in when it is lukewarm.
As good a drink as any preparation, if people would only " cultivate " the taste for it, is cool, pure water.
FAULTY COW FEEDING. One of the most serious faults in the dairy

methods of the present day is in the general feeding of the cows—feeding each and all alike, and about the same amount, whether large or small, in heavy milk or stripping, and far too often feeding two cows side by side with no par- titions between them, and allowing the larger and stronger cow to monopolise the feed. It has been demonstrated, says "Farm and Home," that the best dairymen of the day are those who feed and treat their cows as though thay had a collection of one-cow dairies, treating each cow and feeding her as though she- was the sole study of her owner. Those men who are feed- ing animals for show purposes soon find that some of them needsto be fed more often than others. Some need more starch and bulky food; others give better yields of milk on a ration con- taining more albuminoid matter. Some cold- blooded cows need more fuel in the way of car- bonaceous foods to keep up bodily heat. Often cows to do their best want water a dozen times in the 24 hours, and here and there a cow mill do quite as well on a single draught daily. All this ought to be studied. Even when kept in the house in winter, not all cows, stable as one will to secure comfort, will do alike., Some need to be turned out on pleasant days, and some do far better allowed to keep in. All this is in the province of the dairyman to find out, and in finding out he will make money. Some dairies do better when the cows get two full feeds a day; others, receiving no more food, but receiving three or four feeds, show an improvement. The best dairying in the future will be of the kind that treats each cow as a single member of the herd, and not use the animals as a collective dairy.

div.head: VALUE OF PEAT.
div.p: THE VALUE OF PEAT.

, Although peat in its various forms is of very , . great commercial value, its use in anTiculture • has not yet been fully appreciated. Its main virtue consists of the humus it contains, and 4 44 i its power of retaining moisture, though there are some samples, particularly from low-lying lands, which undoubtedly possess a useful per- centage of manurial products, a fact substan- tiated by the fine crops of potatoes, carrots, celery, and other vegetables that are raised in some peat districts. Worked into light gravelly or sandy soils, whether for vegetables, flowers, or farm crops, peat has a wonderful effect in maintaining steady growth during drought. Used in this way, it also enables one to apply artificials with more enduring effect, since it holds these plant foods, preventing them from being washed away by rain before root action' can derive the benefit of them: -Thus a direct economy can be practised—an economy that appeals to most of us in these days when manures of all kinds are scarce, and the necet: eity of getting as much as possible out of the land is so great. The best kind of peat to use is that usually cut for fuel in many places. This ia black and crumbly,- yet fairly fibrous, and it generally underlies the "moss," which is of comparatively little value until decom- posed or used as an absorbent of manure water. On a large nursery and market garden where I have lately been engaged, an immense stratum of this black peat was aecidentally discovered underlying two feet of clay—an un- usual formation. As a large part of the garden soil consisted of hot, shaley loam, very apt to dry tip quickly in summer, this peat was ap- plied to it in addition to the ordinary course of manuring. The result was most surprising, not only vegetables, but nursery stuff of all kinds deriving marked benefit. Doubtless the cost of the transit is an obstacle to the more general use of peat in agriculture in some dis- tricts, but there are many places where an inexhaustible supply is within reach, and where it can be secured for next to nothing. Yet it is not appreciated as it ought to be.— "A.T.J.," in Farm and Home.,'"

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
WATERING IN DRY WEATHER.

Many people run away with the idea that if the surface of the soil is moist all is well, and that the plants which have been watered have been sufficiently moistened, whereas in too many cases scarcely a drop has reached the lowermost roots. This giving driblets of water does more harm than good, as it only hardens the surface and checks evaporation. • In the case of very large strong growing herbaceous plants, as phloxes, chrysanthemum leucanthemum, funkias, and such like, the best way is to take out all the soil round the plants, forming this into a ridge, and fill the opening two or three times with water. When the water has soaked away replace the excavated soil. Then a mulch of manure should be laid all round, thus shield- ing the soil from the sun and drying winds. In sloping borders it is almost impossible to give sufficient water 'unless the soil on the lower side of the plant is hollowed out, this preventing the water running to waste. In the case of sloping ground I have found it a good plan to loosen the soil all over and apply a mulch of manure; this mulch retaining sufficiently long any water that may be given to allow it finding its way into the soil.—Wick in "Farm and Home.'

div.head: BLACK CURRANT.
div.p: THE BLACK CURRANT.

In the north the black currant is highly valued, and those who attend to the bushes in the way of feeding well and retain plenty young wood find the crop very profitable—in fact the demand generally is far greater than the supply. A sudden frost will very often mar the prospects of a heavy crop of apples or pears, but it is very seldom that the black currant ,s injured. Healthy bushes which have escaped the dreaded mite will go on for years cropping freely. Even when they are very old it is often possible to reinvigorate black currant bushes by a drastic removal of all the old wood, and careful retention of the young wood that springs from the bottom of the bushes. In my younger days I have distinct, recollections of an old ad seemingly worn out lot of bushes that, after being treated as above, and given a good mulch of manure, grew away freely and bore heavy crops of fine fruit for years afterwards. When the plants are too far exhausted to be worth retaining them, it is a very easy matter to re- place with young trees, which can be easily raised from cuttings.

div.head: LOCAL FACTS AND FANCIES.
div.p: LOCAL FACTS AND FANCIES.
By CRITIC.
We have now entered into the third year ef the war, and the work of destruction still con- tinues.
May the year bring with it the glory of an early peace.
Last Monday was celebrated in a mixed fashion. Several firms still "carried on," and others took the advantage of giving their workers a little relaxation.
Nevertheless we had our fair number of visi- tors, who kept things "merry and bright."
Considerable amusement was caused, when, late on Saturday night, a party of visitors com- menced dancing and singing in the centre of the village.
To see the " Fox-trot " being executed on cobble stones is rather an unusual sight.
Why did several of our leading tradespeople close their establishments without previously informing the general public?
I see that our worthy Council have decided to discontinue the payments to single soldier employes.
Why not take the cases on their merits? There are many single men With quite as heavy responsibilities as married men.
A few months ago the cry was "Single men do your duty,". and I venture to ask if this is the way we are going to allow them to be treated when they have done their duty? " Fair play is bonny play." .
They have at last decided to allow boats to be placed on the lake.
Bowling seems to be the present craze, judg- ing by the large crowd that frequents the principal greens.
The Green Dragon Bowling Club are to hold their fifth handicap for members next Saturday.
How to create a good impression on the spec- tators of a bowling green is simply told:—
Firstly, give a fellow player 5 in 11, and take off your coat.
Secondly, deliver your bowl with a sweeping movement off the right hand and look serious.
Thirdly, follow up your bowl, direct it by word of mouth, and if it does not stop toliching the " jack " begin to swear.
Fun and frolic reigned supreme at the Con- gregational sports last Wednesday.
A novel way of celebrating a birthday has just come to my hearing.
A well-known lady connected with the Con- gregational Church gave ten shillings towards the children's sports prizes in honour of her birthday.
A motor car laden with tarts and pasties collided with, the Bull's Head Hotel window on Thursday morning.
Its " sweetness " was overcoming
Nevertheless it succeeded in wrecking the whole window pane, and in doing extensive damage to its -own body.

Church Trip Postponed.—The Parish Church Sunday School scholars' trip, which was to have taken place to-day, has been indefinitely post- poned, owing to the death and funeral of Mr. A. W. Callender, the well-known church worker. Fishing Tickets.—The Lymm Council have decided that any ratepayer who, after August Bth, spends ss. in day or weekly tickets, shall be entitled to fish in the Lake for the rest of the season free from further cost. Intercession Service.—An intercession service was held at the Congregational Church on Sun- day evening, conducted by the Rev. E. E. Lovell, Baptist minister, who took for his text "The Lord is in the whirlwind and -the storm." The service was well attended. Special hymns were sung.

Local D.C.M. Discharged as Medically Unfit. —Quartermaster-Sergeant T. W. Field, our local D.C.M.. has this week returned home dis- charged from the Army as medically unfit. It is the finish of a glorious soldiering career, a career that has left his name inscribed on the roll of fame. The strain of the privations he endured while in the Dardanelles, and espe- cially during the memorable stand he made for several days whilst wounded in several places, for which he was granted the coveted honour, 'has told its tale, and although he has recbived the best of treatment, it has left him no longer fit for service. He is at present enjoying a well- earned rest, and hopes in the near future to take up some light clerical work. Wesleyan Scholars' Trip to Heaton Park.— The scholars and friends of the Wesleyan Sun- day school held their annual excursion on Wednesday afternoon, and the place selected was Heaton Park, Manchester. The party, numberinc, about 70, journeyed by train from Lymnt to *Broadheath, .where a special tramcar had been reserved, conveying them direct to Heaton 'Park. On arriving at Heaton Park they were met by 'Corporal S. Linley and a few more Lymm soldiers, who conducted them round the principal places of attraction, including the trenches made by convalescent soldiers and placed on exhibition in favour of a local war fund; the huts in which our soldiers live; the lake; and the spaci,ous grounds. After tea, an- other visit was made to the huts, and a short concert was held under the auspices of Mr. John Brazendale, the eminent local concert organiser. Congregational Scholars' Field Day.—The Congregational Sunday school scholars and friends held their annual field day on Wednes- day afternoon in the grounds adjoining the C.T.C. farm. During the afternoon the party, which numbered about 140, assembled in the large field and partook of games. Tea was pro- vided in the refreshment-room adjoining the farm, and was ably served by Mrs. Joseph Egerton and her staff. After tea the sports were conducted by Messrs. D. Holt and George Willan. The principal race of the day was the mothers' race, which created considerable amusement, and was eventually won by Mrs. E. Walker. As the shades of evening were drawing .nigh the party assembled and sang their anniversary hymns and the National Anthem. The singing of the National Anthem terminated a most enjoyable afternoon. Private Arthur Saville as a Cricketer.—At a recent meeting of the Lancashire County Cricket Club Committee it was reported that many members were doing their bit at .the Front, and thanks were received from the Front for gifts of cricket gear sent out by the com- mittee. Lieut. G. F. Jones Williams, in the course of one of these letters of thanks, describes a match Lancashire v. The Rest. "We played -our first match," he says, "just before we came down here—two sides out of the Transport, Lancashire v. The Rest. A most exciting match. The Rest made 101 and Lanca- shire 96, so The Rest won by five _runs. We have a very hot side in the Transport. Two good bats, Hilton and Irwin, Manchester Gram- mar School boys, and one really good class bowler, Bligh, nephew of the Hon. I. Bligh, and quite good enough ,to play for Somerset. Our next match was Transport v. B Company Royal Fusiliers, a side got up by one of the members of your county club, Saville, who has since been wounded. He is a young fellow you ought to watch, 61t. sin., and very nice action, and bowls very fast, and quite worth a trial, as , he can hit, too. They made 41 and knocked us out for 37, and we each made ).08 second innings, so had another very exciting match." "Saville" is Private Arthur Saville, whose wounding was reported in "The Examiner" a fortnight rgo.

div.p: PRIVATE THOMAS WIBBERLEY.
Vi ell-known Lymm Soldi2r Wounded By Shrapnel.

News has this week been received to the effect that Private Thomas Wibberley, of the Che- shire Regiment, has been wounded during the advance. The fact was learned through the medium of a letter sent by a comrade to his father, Mr. Joseph Wibberley, who now resides at Lower Walton, Stockton Heath, and read as follows:

"I am writing to inquire if you have heard about your son, Tom, being wounded. You must not worry yourself about him, for I don't think the wound is bad. He was hit just above the right knee with a piece .of shrapnel. If he has written to you will you kindly send me his address, as I have a lot of letters here belong- ing to him that want re-addressing? Being his pal I have missed him very much since he went, but I shall be very glad to hear that he has got to England. I have just received a letter be- longing to him from you, and I hope that you
Wounded

will excuse me opening it, as I did not know your address and thought it my duty to inform you about Tom's misfortune. I will now close, trusting that poor Tom has had the luck to get home." Private Thomas Wibberley is a well-known local lad and for several years was connected with the local Territorials. At the commence- ment of the war he was mobilised with this corps, but was refused for service as medically unfit. After several subsequent attempts to enlist he was at last accepted and went into training with the Cheshire Regiment and was eventually drafted out to France. During his stay in France he has met sevezal of his old comrades belonging to the local Territorials. He is 22 years of age and was educated at the Lymm and Statham Schools, and worshipped at the Primitive Methodist Church. Prior to the war he was employed as a:farm hand by Mr. William Norcott, Manor Farm, Statham.

div.head: MILITARY TRIBUNAL.
div.p: MILITARY TRIBUNAL.
An Ex-Warrior's Successful
Appeal.
Chairman: Mr. Samuel Gould. Military representative: Mr. F. E. Evans. Tradesman Gets Until December. I

A master baker, grocer and provision dealer, ,and sub-postmaster, applied for total exemption on the ground that he would suffer serious hard- ship if called to 66 Colours, owing to having no one to placein charge. He was a married man with three Young children, and was 39 years 'of age. He also stated that he took an active part in the business both inside and outside. . The Chairman: What staff have you?—Four. One under military age, one over, one rejected, and a female. ,
Do you do any baking?—l assist in the bake- house.
The Military Representative: Does not the lady asEdstant look after the post office?—Yes, she does when I am out, but Tam responsible.
Conditional exemption until Ist .December, subject to joining the V.T.C.
An Aunt's Illness.

A brieksetter (34), who appealed on personal grounds, stated that his chief reasons for asking for exemption were (a) that his aunt was ill and his wife looked after her, and (b) that the separation allowance was not enough to live on. The Chairman: Does your aunt live with you? —'No.
. Well, how does that interfere with you?— There istr one else to look after her but my wife.
How often does she attend her?—Every day. Have you ever thought what your Army allow- ance would he?—Yes, and I am of the opinion that it is insufficient.
Temporary exemption until 4th October, sub- ject to no other appeal being made. Dairyman's Liabilities.

A dairyman (32), who applied for exemption on business grounds, stated that since his last appeal he had had his business on sale, and up to the time of lodging the present appeal he had not had a single applicant. Altogether, includ- ing debts, he had invested in the business A:296, and if he were called to the Colours all would be lost. He was a married man and delivered all the milk himself. Applicant stated that if he sold the business he would inform the Tribunal.
Conditional exemption until Ist December, subject to joining the V.T.C. Over 12 Months Fighting the Hun.

A time-expired soldier appeared to ask for exemption on personal grounds. Mr. G. L. Welford, who represented appli- cant, stated that his client was 30 years old, was a bricksetter by trade, and worked for a Warrington firm. • He was a time-expired soldier and had already done his bit. Altogether, he had served 11 years and four months in the Army, and his time expired on the 31st of March last. He was then holding the rank of Lance-Sergeant. He was called up in August, 1914, and after training about six months in England he was sent to France. He was sent to the trenches seven days after he landed, and remained there until he received his discharge. "The fact of him accepting his discharge was through the death of his father, which took place while he was in France, and which left his mother, who is infirm, unprovided for," said Mr. Welford. "I think it is a case where you might grant total exemption, seeing that he has alieady done his share."' The Chairman: Has he taken Into considera- tio4 what dependant's allowance his mother would get?—Yes, 9s. 4d., what she got prior to his coming out. At first the amount was only 7s. 9d., but when his father died it was in. creased to 9s. 4d. The Military Representative (addressing applicant) : Were you ever ill while on active service?—Yes, I was 16 days in ,hospital. Temporary exemption until Ist December. Salt Works' Cases.

A sequel to the Salt Works' cases which were adjourned sine die pending an application for badges took place at the last sitting. A re- presentative of the firm appeared to inform the Tribunal that all had been granted badges but one, and the Tribunal taking into considera- tion that this man was forty years of age and had eight children granted him conditional exemption. subject to joining the Voluntary Trainin:; Corps.

div.head: PRIVATE ARTHUR STATHAM.
div.p: PRIVATE ARTHUR STATHAM.
Very Nasty Wound In The Leg In
The Advance.

News has this week been received to the effeet that another Lymm. soldier has been wounded in the advance. A letter sent by Private Arthur Statham, the Cheshire Regiment, and re- ceived by his mother, Mrs. J. Statham, at Mos- ton-street, Newfields (sent from the "George of Russia" Heatherdene Hospital, Harrogate), reads as follows: "I am lying here sufferihg from a very nasty wound, but do not worry, as it is doing fine. I can tell you it has made a nice little hole through my leg. lam very glad to get away from the trenches for a bit, for the noise of the big guns was almost driving me 'daft.' I siippose you have been wondering where I was while I was in France. Well, I was at been talking about): that was where the Ger- mans made me a present of a piece of shell. This is a fine hospital and bflongs to a Russian duchess, who runs it entl42o.ly herself. She comes round every day and chats with the patients. We can have anything we want if we will only ask for it. I have a long tale to tell you when I come home, for I was in the big 'fight on July Ist, and had a very narrow escape from death.".

Private Arthur Statham prior to the war was connected for several years with the local Ter- ritorials. He is 26 years of age, and was edu- cated at Lymm School and worshipped at the Congregational Church. He enlisted in March, 1915, and was drafted out to France in February, 1916. He was well known in sporting

circles, and was a member of the local football club. Prior to enlisting he was employed by the Urban District Council in the sanitary department. His brother, Private . Jack Statham, has paid the supreme sacrifice, and his brother-in-law, Private Fred Percival, is at present ill with fever at Salonica.

div.head: PRIVATE J. FRED PERCIVAL.
div.p: PRIVATE J. FRED PERCIVAL.
Down With Fever, But Considers Himself Lucky.

Mrs. Fred Percival, Moston-street, Newfields, has this week received news to the effect that her husband, Private Fred Percival, Cheshire Regiment, who is serving in the East, is ill in hospital suffering from fever. A letter received from the gallant soldier says :—" I am at pre- sent ill in hospital suffering with fever, but hope to get well again before long. I suppose you have heard about brother Sam (another Lymm soldier) having the fever? In fact, there is hardly a man who has not been down with it, but thank God there it not so !natty dying. Our Sam I believe has gon- tAown to the base, convalescent, and I believe that he is all right again. I was very sorry to hear about your brother Jack being kilted (meaning Private Jack Statham) and poor 'Henry Brookes. It is very hard lines, and I think that I am a very lucky man to come from France alive, for I can assure you it was a very hot shop?' A further letter, dated 26th July, and received this week, stated that the fever had taken all the strength away from him, but he was fast recovering. Private Fred Percival for son.« considerable time served in the old Militia. He is 34 years of age, and is a married man with two children. He was educated at Lynim School and wor- shipped at the Congregational Church. He enlisted in March, 1915, and was drafted out to France in June of the same year, taking part in the fighting round Loos, where he was wounded. After recuperating at a base hospital he was drafted out to the East. Prior to enlist-
ing he was employed as a tanner by the Grap- penhall Tanning Company.

div.head: NEW DEPARTURE.
div.p: A NEW DEPARTURE.
Boating To Be Allowed By Council On Lymm Lake.

When Von Moltke looked upon London, Paris, or sonie other .big place that -wasn't his he ex- claimed unavailingly, "What a city to loot!" and when people have gazed upon the spacious anti beautiful lake at Lymm they have thought enviously. "What a setting for boat- ing !" That sentiment, 'too, has been unavail- ing until now. For years the Windermere of Cheshire has been unrippled and unbriifhtened by ships that pass either day or night, and wanderers by its side have often sighed for the time when the simple beauty of the water would be crowned with gently-sailing boats washed by the waves, and containing those whose happy laughter would sound in unison with the chirping of the birds in the leafy trees. The Urban Council now, being the owners of the lake and having got their bearings, see the reasonableness of boating. For a long time on Monday night they sat discussing the matter in committee, relegating "The Examiner" man to an ante-room to await the momentous decision, " to boat or not to boat."

At last when summoned to enter the august Council Chamber the following minute was read and passed: "That private rowing boats be allowed on the lake at the rate of £3 per annum, including the privilege of fishing from the boat, and that private motor boats be allowed at the rate of £5 per annum."

There was no speech-making, no joyous ex- clamation at the prospect of getting aboard in the heart of Cheshire, no talk of dressing up one of the Councillors as Father Neptune at the first launching ceremony. There was just the mere proposing, seconding and adopting. It was like a condolence resolution, passed in silence and standing—for the tired Councillors were getting up to go home. A great oppor- tunity to advertise Lymna's best attraction in the presence of "The Examiner" man was thus missed.
But, perhaps, they wanted to stroll along the banks of the lake to select at once a site for their own boathouses.

div.head: THOSE ALLOWANCES.
div.p: THOSE ALLOWANCES.
Council Revise Their Scheme For
Soldier-Employes.

A decision to alter the scheme of allowancds to their employes who have joined the Army was arrived at by the Urban District Council at a special meeting on Monday evening, Coun- cillor F. Lockyer presiding. Previously, all employes have been paid half wages, but now payments to .single men will be discontinued and married men's allowanPes will be made up to the ordinary wages. There was no discussion at the Council meet- ing, the matter having been thrashed out at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee.

div.head: RELIGION TO SAVE SOCIETY.
div.p: RELIGION TO SAVE SOCIETY.

"We are now within measurable distance of a situation which no power of the sword, which no amount .or quality of legislation are possible to cope with—the return of peace to which we are all looking forward so eagerly," declared the Rector of Lymm in this month's Magazine. "It is at this juncture that we are reminded on every hand that peace has its dangers as well as war, and that there is only one power, the power of religion, that can keep Us safe for the future. Religion has saved society more than once in days gone by, it saved for example the world in the breaking up of the Roman Empire, and it can save us to-day if Christians can find the power there is in it to lift and inspire their lives and bind them together in a bond which all the sin and selfishness of the world is unable to break."

div.head: £l5O WAR SAVINGS.
div.p: £l5O WAR SAVINGS.

"The appeal in Lymm Parish Magazine. in connection with the War Savings Certificates .met with some response," the Rector writes. "The membership has now reached its first century and the number of certificates pur- chased by the Lymm Branch since its inception less than four months ago is one hundred and ninety-three, the amount paid in being £l5O. All this is to the good of the country, and we may also add to the good of the depositors, who will find the benefit of their savings in time to come. But primarily the movement is a patrio- tic one, our men have offered the free sacrifice of themselves for their country, the munition workers are sacrificing their time and strength that the armies may be well supplied with the necessary war material for carrying on the campaign to a successful issue, and in the third line of defence stand the civilians and non- combatants, who are earnestly asked to make the essential sacrifice of comforts and luxury without which those other sabrifices will be of no avail."

div.head: LOSS TO LYMM.
div.p: LOSS TO LYMM.
Death Of Mr. A. W. Callender,
J.P.

With regret we announce the death of Mr. A. W. Callender, J.P., which took place at his residence, West View House, in the early hours of Thursday morning, in his 66th year. The late gentleman had been in indifferent health for some time, but had only been confined to bed for a brief period. What his loss means to Lymm only those who knew him can tell. He took a prominent part in most public matters, and had been Connected with the Church for the greater part of his life. Two years ago, on resigning from the position of churchwarden, -he was presented with a beauti- ful gold watch in recognition of over thirty years of faithful service. Even when he re- signed this office he continued to be an active member of the Church Council. Apart from his Church duties he took an active interest in politics in favour of the Conservative party, and held the office of secretary for the Lymm Con- servative Club and Association. He • was also Conservative agent for this polling district and a -meinber of the Executive Council of the Altrincham Division Conservative Association. His father, Mr. Roemaine Callender, was for some considerable time a Conservative M.P. for Manchester. Mr. A. W. Callender was also a foundation manager of the Parochial Schools. In business he practised as a commission agent in the wino and spirit trade. As a mark of deep respect the Church flag has been placed half-mast.
The funeral will take place to-day at the Parish Church at 3.30 p.m. It is expected to be fully choral.

An Exchanged Prisoner.—Private Joseph Antrobus, the Cheshire Regiment, who was re- ported in "The Examiner" to be a wounded prisoner, has returned- to England in the last batch of exchanged prisoners, and is at present in the Queen Alexandra Hospital at London. His brother, Harry, who was wounded as stated in last week's issue, has also landed in England. Their home address is Yeald Brow, Statham. Both aro reported to be doing well.

Council Chairman's Son-inAaw Wounded.— We regret to announce that Private Wm. Hynch, Manchester Regiment, has been seriously wounded in the head. The news came in a telegram sent to his wife at Statham by the military authorities. The gallant soldier was exceedingly well-known and highly res- pected. and the news of his misfortune will be grieved by a large circle of friends. He is a son-in-law to Councillor Frederick Lockyer, the present Council chairman. . Motor Van Crashes Into Hotel Window.—On Thursday morning a motor van driven by a lady ran into the window of the Bull's Head Hotel. The van, which was owned by a War- rington confectioners' firm, was proceeding up Lymm Bridge. While attempting to back out of the way of another vehicle coming in the opposite direction, the brakes failed and the van crashed into the Bull's Head Hotel win- dow, a drop of several feet from the road level. Although the shock was great the driver escaped injury, but extensive damage was done to the window and the car. By the help of several men the van was extricated from the wreckage and towed to a neighbouring yard.

Extension of Unemployment Insurance.—All munition workers of every deseription have now to be insured against unemployment, and the work of meeting the great demand for books has fallen very heavily on the hands of local officials. Calling at the local Labour Exchange, Bridgewater-street, early this week, our repre- sentative found it quite a hive of industry. The legal agent, Mr. Arthur Sutton. was making the necessary preparations for the issue of a large number of new books. To avoid delay all concerned are advised to make an early appli- cation.

Seven persons were summoned at the Dares- bury Sessions on Wednesday for allowing exposed lights in their dwelling-houses after dark, and, with one exception, were each fined 2s. 6d.

In the one case referred to, the defendant said that owing to his wife's illness the doctor had given him instructions to keep a light burning during the night. He had not drawn the blind, as the window was open to admit air. He produced the lamp—a tiny affair—which he said was burning when the officer called. Acting-Sergeant Worth said defendant did not give him the explanation just made, and Superintendent Owen told the magistrates that if the fact had been known the charge would not have been put forward. div.p: A PICTURISED ROMANTIC NOVEL BY ROY L.McCARDELL ADAPTED FROM THE SENSATIONAL "FLYING SERIAL FILM BY ALEC J. BRAID.
racters in this story are purely imaginary, living SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS.

Colonel Arthur Stanleigh and Judge Lamar Stan- Cousins, of Virginia, are bitter enemies over •the possession of The Diamond from he Sky. COlonel Stanleigh, when a daughter is born, buys the male heir of a gipsy king, that he may keep the iewel. He plans to rear Esther, the girl, in secrecy. Esther and The Diamond from the Sky are stolen by Hagar, the gipsy mother. Years later Hagar returns Esther and the diamond, but of the old group only Dr. Lee is living. Blair Stanleigh kills Dr. Lee and steals the jewel. Then Blair Stanleigh and Arthur Stanleigh, the false heir, fight a duel. Arthur, thinking he has killed his cousin, flees in a racing motor ear and has an accident. He is found bY Esther and Hagar and nursed to health. Hagar tells him his real identity. Arthur swears to make himself worthy of Esther and leaves, taking the diamond. 'Blair takes him to a grand ball, where they meet Vivian Mazston, a New York belle, wear- ing the diamond. It is stolen. A greater confusion than that caused by the loss of the diamond arises When the Sheriff of Fairfax demands the arrest of Arthur Stanleigh. He escapes, and finds work and refuge as a farm hand. Luke Lovell drops the diamond into a mailbag. The gem clings by its clasp to a rent in the bag, and is afterwards found by Quabba, the hunchback organ-grinder. He does not retain it long; Clarence, his monkey, drops it in an owl's nest_ Arthur, working on a farm as "John Powell" masks himself and goes to the Fairfax tournament, where he wins the highest honour. Ilagar, holding proofs of Blair Stanleigh's guilt, is brutally attacked by the young man ancl•her mind destroyed. The diamond finds its way to a Chinese oDium den whence Blair steals it. Vivian marries him and they escape from Toni Blake in a train whicb robbers board, and take the diamond with other jewels and money. Pursued by a Sheriff's 4___-Dosse the train robbers lose the diamond and 41-"Aure, the latter being found by 4' John Powell."
CHAPTER XI
THE WEB OF DESTINY.

Such a wonderful find was destined to make a great change in Arthur Stanleigh's mode Of life. Re did not trouble himself with the reason for the Presence of a large sum of money on the Prairie. Re would oontinue to be known as "John Powell," and Perhaps the day would come when he could Claim Esther as his wife.. If good fortune was favouring Arthur Stanleigh, hie cousin Blair was 'sick at heart. All his plans hacl fallen to the giourid, and although he was re- turning to his mother at Richmond, he did not view the prospect with delight. He dreaded his !nether's tongue. Spurned and derided by Mrs. Lamar Stanleigh, Luke Lovell was seeking either Blair or Arthur. Convinced that one or othez would be glad to pay hina for knowledge of the Stanleigh secret, he did not care which paid him his price. - "I can sell you the Stanleigh secret," he said to Blair, whom he met returning to_Richmond: _
"Go away," said Blair. "I do not wish to buy any secrets yon may hold. What can you know of the Stanleigh secret anyway?" _

"Then you won't deal?." "No I will not. I decline to have anything to do With a gipsY." "You are a fool! You will not pay me'. but I know someone who will pay heavily if I do not tell, and I am going to him." What does he mean? asked Blair of himself, and for a moment he thought of recalling the man who was striding away in anger. Then he shrugged his shoulders and made his way to Mrs. Ran- dolph' s beautiful house. One day Mrs. Stanleigh called Esther to her. " Your mother does not appear to get better," she said to the girl. "We must do something, and I Will pay the expense of an operation to restore her reason if the surgeons think it can be done." "Oh. thank you. I must accept your offer, it is dreadful to see mother in the state she is. I can- not think what can have happened to her," replied the grateful girl. Thoroughly deceived by the woman. Esther joy- fully accompanied Hagar to the sanatorium; but Quabba, wise in the wiles of the world, doubted Mrs. Stanleigh, and her remark to the surgeon Droved that his judgment was not at fault. "Let me know before you operate. Something May prevent me from defraying the cost," said she. Choosing the tramps' method of travelling, Luke Lovell boarded .a goods train, and all -went well until he was discovered. Then the usual thing happened. Luke was thrown off the train and stranded in an arid plain. He wandered dejectedly towards the nearest settlement until thirst sapped his strength and a mirage threatened to deprive him of reason. Summoning his last reserves of deter- mination, he staggered along until with a cry of delight he saw The Diamond from the Sky on the sand at his feet. Once more he clasped the precious gem, and then the snake which had been the diamond's guardian since it had fallen from the hand of the train robber bit him. With a shriek he flung, the snake and gem from him and lay down in agony to die. Enfeebled by thirst he now had to combat the virulence of a poison, and Luke Lovell knew that failing rescue his hours were numbered.

Across the plains came a galloping horseman. " John Powell' had hidden his wealth, all save a 101 l of notes, and was riding back to the farm to throw up his job. Moaning and stirring on the Pound before him was a gipsy whom he had seen before.

"Wafer! Snake!" whispered the stricken man, and divining what had happened. Arthur gave him drink, and then hurried Luke to the camp, where a draught of potent spirit revived him and the snake bite was treated. The gipsy was yet to live to do 'What mischief he could. "I can sell you a secret,' saii Luke the follow- ing morning. "Something you ought to know. Are You willing to deal?" ", What secret can you F.ll to me?"

" The Stanleigh secret." 'Why should I buy the -Stanleigh secret, what- ever it is? I am not a Stanleigh; my name is John Powell.' " "I know different. You call yourself Arthur Stanleigh, but you are not. You are Hagar's son, and your name is Harding. You are going to pay to keep that dark." Deecoceef,oe
)00CCI

and have no connection with or relation to any person.] "I should have let you die, but the fact that I am not Arthur Stanleigh must be kept secret until my mother chooses to speak. Here are five hundred dollars. Take the money and keep your mouth shut." Arthur handed the man a roll of notes in the centre of which was a Wells Fargo bond for the amount.

Before Blair Stanleigh reached Richmond his mother had sent for Abe Bloom to ascertain the truth concerning Vivian Marston and her past. "Oh. Vivian is a smart New yorker. and I am not sure she is not married to a gentleman crook. At any rate, she is an adventuress," was Abe's reply- _ _ _ _

"I thought so," chuckled .the delighted widow, and he had further cause for satisfaction when a firm of solicitors wrote: "Do not worry about your son's secret marriage to Vivian Marston. It can- not possib.., be legal, as her first husband is alive and undivorced."

Consequently, when like a whipped cur Blair re- turned, his mother held all the trumps. "You are a fine son," was her greeting. "First you rob your mother and then marry an adven- turess, but above all you have again lost the diamond. Don't you understand that you have the Earldom of Stanleigh within your grasp?" the irate woman asked.
"No, I don't, and bow dare you call Vivian an adventuress?"
"Because she is; read that," handing him the letter.
With an oath Blair tore up the letter and asked "What am I to do?"
"To do? Marry Esther. There are reasons why you must. I know you are going to say she is a ' • -'- - is nothing of the kind. Esther is of equal birth with yourself."

. - All his life through Blair had _followed his raother'a advice in matters relating to the Stanleigh feud, and if by marrying Esther he could advance the interests of the family and his own he was content to throw Vivian over. Blair was already in doubt as to the wisdom of the hasty marriage, and know- ledge of a. previous marriage opened the way to the wooing of Esther. Now that she knew Arthur was not her brother. Esther's whole love was for him. Blair's attempts at love-making met with no re- sponse, but he was not easily repulsed. One morn- ing he accompanied the girl on a ride, and the whole way pestered her with assurances of his love. "I do not want your love. I am quite happy as I am; besides I could not love you." "But I intend that you shall love me," he said, and would have seized her had not Quabba, the watchful, steppea forward. "You are annoying this lady," said the hunch- back, as the girl spurred her horse and rode away. "Get out of the way you hunchback gipsy," shouted Blair, striking Quabba on the head with his riding crop and cantering after the girl. "You brute, dearly shall you pay for this," shouted Quabba,

All the way home Blair pressed his attentions upon Esther. and the girl. heart-sick and distressed. went to Mrs. Stanleigh and complained. Her recep- tion was not an encouraging one. " Ybu should feel honoured by my son's attentions. You are nothing but_a_gim beggar."

Mrs. Stanleigh had yet another card to play- If Esther persisted in her refusal to regard Blair's suit with favour, the widow would see what could be done by threatening to withdraw her assistance in curing Hagar. "I have had a letter from the sanatorium asking for a guarantee of a thousand dollars before an operation can be performed. lam not sure that I can spare such a large sum." With this 'thrust in her bosom the girl, bursting with grief, went to her room to have a good cry and formulate a scheme. "But what can Ido without money?" she asked herself pitifully. In the extremity of her need Esther remembered Quabba. It was understood between them that whenever she needed assistance a rose in the win- dow of her bedroom would be a signal. If ever she needed,va friendly advice, Esther needed one now, and, taking a. rose from the bowl the girl hung out the signal.

The darkest ;loud has its silver lining, and good news was even at that moment on its way. Mrs. Stanleigh, fearful lest Esther should be approached by friends, had given orders that no letters were to reach the girl before she had been Consulted, but the coloured maid, won by the pathetic, wistful face of the sweet girl, held, other views on the matter. Coming quietly into the room she said: " Dat old Mrs. Stanleigh said to give her any letter that come for you. But I didn't, Honey."
It was a letter from Arthur. "I am making arrangements to clear my name of all the mysteries surrounding it. For the present I must remain away .from those .I Iove.—ARTHUR."
"The rose is in the window. Clarence. That is the signal for us." remarked Quabba, coming up the road, and Clarence climbed up the trellis to acquaint Esther of their arrival.
Looking out, she called down to her faithful friend: "Wait for me here, to-night," and when night fell. man, maid and monkey went back to the gipsy encampment. _

Although the sum he found was a big one, Arthur Stanleigh did not intend remaining idle. The fame of the Californian oilfields was spreading, and he decided to invest all he could spare in an oil well. With that purpose in view, he purchased the Fair Hope property. It was an. astonishing purchase, because the boring had not yielded a pint of oil; although considerable sums had been spent upon its development. Hope, however, burnt brightly in "John Powell's " breast. The future held no dread for him. His ambition was to clear his name of the suspicion of having killed Dr. Lee, and marry the girl whose winsomeness had enslaved his heart. Three people were crossing the plain that had nearly proved fatal to Luke Lovell. An Indian squaw and her fire-water-loving husband toiled along, and behind him trudged Luke. The gipsy had already squandered the money given him by Arthur, and, destitute, he remembered the diamond. Criss-cross he traversed the place where he imag- ined he had found and lost the great diamond. Ahead of him walked the Indian woman. The glitter of a jewel attracted her. There in the dust lay The Diamond from the Sky, and the same night, while the disappointed Luke was sleeping in a hut, the wonderful gem sparkled on the breast of an Indian baby.

IN THE COURTS.
THE MANX CAMP SENSATION.
A Murder Charge.
SERGT. JOHN WILLIAMS GUILTY, BUT INSANE.

At the Court of General Gaol Delivery, which is the 'Manx equivalent of the Assizes, held at Douglas on Tuesday, John Williams (45), a ser- geant in the3o6th Company of the Royal Defence Corps,, variously stated to belong to Liverpool and to have lived at Ship-yard, Warrington; pleaded not guilty to an 'indictment charging him with the wilful murder of Wil- liam Henry Malings •(47), a colour-sergeant in the same company, and who was a married hairdresser living at 269, Liverpool-road. The Attorney-General for the Isle of Man (Mr. G. A. Ring) prosecuted, and Mr. H. P. Kelly, of the Manx Bar, defended. .
Williams's wife was present in Court during the trial, as was Mrs. Malinos and her son and daughter.

The Court was constituted of the Lieutenant- Governor of the Island (Lord Raglan), Deem., ster Moore, and the Clerk of the Rolls (Mr. Thomas Kneen). Outlining the case for the prosecution, the Attorney-General said so far as could be dis- covered there had been no dispute or ill-feeling between the two soldiers. A shot was heard from the sergeants' sleeping quarters and Malings was found bleeding from. the mouth, nose and ears, and evidently dying. Asked if he had sent for a doctor, prisoner answered "No," and began to fill his pipe. Prisoner's rifle was lying on his bed and two of his cartridges were beside it. Williams was,placed under arrest: and later on he voluntarily stated. • in the presence of Colour-Sergeant Harrison, "The cur has been the cause of all my trouble since I have been In the company, and I have made a clean job of it. He is only one of my victims." Subsequently he remarked volun- tarily in the presence of Corporal Phillips, who relieved Harrison, "I am rid of that bastard; I am satisfied."

div.head: PRISONER'S CAREER.
div.p: PRISONER'S CAREER.

Mr. Joseph Madigan, assistant to the Camp Commandant, in reply to the Attorney-General, said prisoner understood what was said to him. Prisoner appeared to have received' a shock. His expression was what witness would expect to find on a man who had just *shot down an- other man, whose dead body was lying on the floor.

Subsequently Mr. Madigan was re-called, at the request of the jury, in connection with cer- tain inquiries he had made as to prisoner's previous career. He said that what he had learned might prejudice prisoner if he stated it.

The Attorney-General: We don't want to go into a rambling inquiry as to prisoner's past life, which might be most unfair to him. You might, however, answer as to whether there is any ground for thinking that he has been on service in hot climates and has had sunstroke.

Witness said he could not say whether pris- oner had had such service. Generally, he could say that the result of his inquiries did not bear out certain statements which prisoner had made as to his former career.

div.head: REQUEST FROM THE DOCK.'
div.p: REQUEST FROM THE DOCK.'
Mr. Kelly contended that the utter absence of motive, combined with prisoner's peculiar demeanour, pointed to his insanity at the time the ,crime was committed.
The jury, after an absence of eighteen min- utes, returned. The Foreman said: The jury find prisoner guilty of murder, but find that' at the time the crime was committed prisoner was of unsound mind.

Deemster Moore, addressing the prisoner, said: In this case the jury have taken a most merciful view. The sentence of• the Court is that you be detained during His Majesty's pleasure. Prisoner: May I make a request or state- ment?
Deemster Moore: Perhaps you had better say nothing. The case is over. - _
Prisoner was then removed. As he left the Court he called out "Good-bye" to his wife.

div.head: PARCEL OF LIES.
div.p: A PARCEL OF LIES.

A fifteen-year-old boy named Albert Bradford, who was before the Borough Magistrates on Friday of last week on a charge of travelling from Dublin without paying his fare, was again brought up on Wednesday. The, Chief Constable said that the boy arrived at Bank Quay Station by a •very early train on Friday morning of last week, and on being asked for his ticket, he said he had not got one. He said he had come from Dublin, and a ticket-collector took him into his office and gave him half of his breakfast. The boy managed to slip away, and while doing so he took with him a ticket from off the ledge. Dur- ing the time of his detention he had told a parcel of lies, and the police doubted whether he had come from Dublin. The boy had be- longed to the St. Ann's Industrial School, Liverpool, for some years, and was licensed out from time to time. As the railway company had no desire to press tile case, he (the Chief Constable) asked that the boy should be handed over to the school. This course was adopted.

div.head: AN ABSENTEE'S DENIAL AND CONFESSION.
div.p: AN ABSENTEE'S DENIAL AND CONFESSION.

Charged at the Borough Police Court on Thursday with being an absentee under the Military Service Act, Edward G. Williams, window cleaner, 18, Holland-street, was fined 40s. and ordered to be handed over to the military authorities. P.C. Vost said that in consequence of informa- tion received from the military authorities he visited • defendant's house on Thursday night and asked Williams why he had not reported. He replied, "I have not received any notice." He subsequently admitted, however, that he had received a notification, but had taken no notice of it.

When a charge of being drunk on licensed premises was brought against James Murray and Daniel Bond, of no settled abode, at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Murray said that during the shoit time he had been in Warrington the, detectives were always follow- ing him about. Both prisoners were fined lfis. or, in default, seven days' imprisonment. . Acting-Sergeant Armstrong said that on *Mon- day night he saw the two prisoners enter a public-house in a drunken condition. lie warned the proprietor not to serve the prisoners, who thereupon left, and 'entered the Old House at Home, where they were arrested.

Charged with working a horse in an unfit con- dition, John H. Gregory. 144,. Winwiek-road, was fined 20s. at the Borough Police Court en Tuesday, the Chairman of the Bench remarking that it was a'serious case.

Inspector Bonham, of the R.S.P.C.A., sard that on the 29th ult. he saw defendant driving. a brown gelding attached to a milk float. Noticing the pour condition of the animal lie stopped the defendant and examined the horse. lie found two raw, discharging wounds, whic.h the saddle and collar were rubbing. div.p: CRICKET.
WARRINGTON AN XI. V. EARLESTOWN.

The Warrington XI. visited the Viaduct enclosure last Saturday, and, considering the strong opposi- tion, made a creditable show. The home team won the toss and commenced in dashing style, J. Craw- ley (77), their opening batatnan, giving a brilliant, if somewhat lucky, display. Thos. Marsh (47) played very carefully without giving a chance, while G. B. Leigh (22), J. Riley (37), J. Valentine (30), and W. Jenkinson (14), although obtaining double figures. were rather fortunate. The fielding of the visitors was wretched, and numerous chances were missed. But for this. Earlestown would have been dismissed for a much smaller total.
Warrington were !eft ninety minutes in which to obtain_ the runs, an 'impossible task. They played a sporting game, however, much good batting being seen.

The feature of the Warrington innings was the promising display given by T. E. Allen (45). Going in at the fall of the fifth wicket, he began very carefully, but later hit with good effect, helping himself to eighteen in one over from Alderson, the Earlestovrn captain. He received a sporting ova- tion on being well taken by J. Crawley in the long field. G. Duckworth (12) played his usual sound game, while F. Lemon (24) and J. Constable (17) were responsible for bright displays, the latter making several fine drives, one of which dropped on the Viaduct Works, doing damage to the glass. Only two minutes remained for play when the visitors' last batsman was dismissed, Earlestown deservedly winning a keen' and interesting game, which seemed to be thoroughly enjoyed by the large crowd. div.head: MILITARY TRIBUNALS.
div.p: MILITARY TRIBUNALS.
VOLUNTEER SERVICE COMPULSORY.
The Town Hall Tribunal, sitting on Tuesday, had an ,exceptionally short list of cases before them, but each appeal received the most careful and prolonged consideration.

div.head: Badged Man Refused.
div.p: Badged Man Refused.

A young man, 18 years of age, appealed for exemption on domestic grounds. He stated that he had a brother on active service who made an allotment of us. 7d. weekly. Applicant, who is employed at the Richmond- Gas Stove and Meter Co., is the principal support of his father, mother and young sister. His father is 68 years old and suffers from heart trouble. He produced his badge. The application was refused, Dr. Joseph (chairman) remarking that the rent of the home would be allowed, and that applicant could make the wad allohnent. • Other Refusals.

A tea salesman. 26, who had been given a month's exemption from the 6th April, again appeared before the Tribunal.' The firm he worked for had not put in any appeal. but he stated that owing to the extent of his district— an eighteen mile radius about Warrington—it would take some time to initiate a successor. In announcing that the application was re- fused the Chairman said that the man had had ample time—more than enough—to make arrangements,

A pawnbroker and clothier appealed for exemption on behalf of a buyer in his ladies' outfitting department. The man is 35 years of age, and exemption had already been given up to the 30th June. The application was refused.

div.head: Bakers' Vanman.
div.p: Bakers' Vanman.

Messrs. Chantry and Son, bakers and con- fectioners, applied to the Tribuitr4, tor exemp- tion in the case of a motor van driver, lie was largely engaged in the delivery of bread to private households. The man, who had been with them over twelve months, is 38 years of age. Efforts had been made to get a girl to take his place, but they had not thought of procuring a man over military age. One month's exemption. " Volunteer" Service " Compulsory."

An insurance agent (40), who Stated that he had been before the Medical Board and passed for "sedentary duties," was informed that he would be granted conditional exemption pro- vided this stateinent was confirmed. The Chairman explained that if conditional exemption were granted applicant would he expected to join the Volunteer Training Corps. This would be the condition. Others, in whose cases the condition had been made, had not joined as they showld have clore. When they knew it was compulsory it might be otherwise.
Master Joiner.

Mr. Forshaw, solicitor, presented the appli- cation of a master joiner and property repairer, aged 39, a married man with family of four. He explained that the only person employed by applicant was a labourer over 60 years of age, and that he would have to close ddwn his business if taken for service. In conjunction with the joinery business he carried out rc- pairs to about two hundred and fifty houses. Conditional exemption—required to. join Voluntary Training Corps.

div.head: Market Garde.
div.p: Market Garde.

A Latchford nurseryman and market gardener, aged 32, married, four years in busi- ness, sought exemption. He cultivates two acres with kitchen vegetables and had a large crop of tomatoes under glass. He worked with- out any assistance, hiq wife looking after the shop. Granted time to end of October, same to be final.

div.head: In the Wire Trati:.
div.p: In the Wire Trati:.
An applicant, who described himself as a wire worker; appealed on business and domestic grounds. Hc is a married man,, with four chil- dren, and had started business in tie autumn of .1914.

In reply to Captain Mathams he explained that he made hay-band wire out 0.c.. scrap pur- chased by him from various firms. He had one man (25) helping, who has been rejected by thp Army as medically unfit. Temporary exemption was granted (final) to the end of September. A Coachbuildcr's Application.

Mr. Heywood, coachbuilder and wheelwright, appealed on behalf of two of his men, one aged 38, a widower, who worked as a wheelwright, and the other as painter's labourer, 37, who is apparently a first class hand at coach painting. Conditional exemption was granted in both cases.

div.head: SINGLE MEN'S PLEAS.
div.p: SINGLE MEN'S PLEAS.
Tribunal Takes Up Firm Attitude.

Several single men renewed their applica- tions for an extension of the temporary exemp- tion at the Tribunal at the Town Hall on Thursday, the Deputy-Mayor presiding, and most interesting dialogues took place. A single man, aged 26 years, in business as a clog and boot maker, came before the Tribuval and asked for an extension. He said he had tried to sell his business by mentioning it to travellers and putting a notice in the window. Captain Mathams: This man was exempted until the 30th June, and he now comes forward having entirely failed to dispose of his business. The Chairman: One way or another you have had eight months. A month's exemption. Final.
Applicant: I am that busy that I could do with another man now.
The Chairman: And the Army could (lc) with • _ you. ----- - - - - -
Like A Married Man.
Declaring that he was in the position of a married man, an applicant, aged 21 years, said his mother had a heart affection.

Captain Mathams pointed out that the appli- cant had been exempted until June 30th and he had already had a month and a half over. Applicant: If I went would my mother get a reasonable allotment? The Chairman: Yes.

Applicant: I have heard of some cases where they have not. It is not a case of my wanting to evade service. I would not mind if she was provided for adequately. The Chairman: We have considered that and believe your mother would have a suitable allowance.
Applicant: Will you give ine.a guarantee?

The Chairman: I could not give you any per- sonal guarantee. Applicant: I am the same as a married man, you know. The Chairman: Well, a married man, aged 21, would stand a good chance of going, you know.
Appeal refused. " Faith In Tribunal's Generosity."

A , plumber, also a single man, of 38 years, admitted, in reply to the Chairman, that he had recently taken on another contract. Captain Mathams :4 You were given exemp- tion until 30th June. You must have had great faith in the generosity of the Tribunal by taking on another contract! Applicant: I am not trying b evade military service any more than anyone else, but there is an important business here. _
The Chairman: In cases like yours larger firms volunteer to carry on the business in your absence. We will adjourn the case to see what can be done. , Coffins and Coffins.

A coffin maker and undertaker, married an'd having no children, sought exemption, and replying to the Chairman, said that on an aver- age he bad 117 private funerals .a year and made 70 coffins for the Union Workhouse.

Captain Matliams: How ,are your Union funerals done?—l just supply the coffins for those who die in the Workhouse and sometimes those in receipt of out-relief. . How long does it take to make a Union coffin?-0f course, there are coffins and coffins. Tbose for the Union it takes about six hours; others it takes longer., Moreover, I have to make ti funeral, arraniements. . . The Chairman: Does your wife .help No, she is no coffin maker. (Laughter.)

given exemption for three months, with leave to appeal further. The Captain's Inference. .

When Messrs. Chadwick and Co., paper bag manufacturers, appealed for a paarried man, aged 26, in the dispatching depaitment, the firm's representative admitted that the man was a bad timekeeper, so Captain Mathams suggested they ought to let him go into the Army. The Representative: That means that we should commit suicide in order to escape worry. Captain Mathams: Are you suggesting it is suicide to join the Army?—No, not at all. Captain Mathams: That was the inference. The Representative: I meant it Would not improve our position by his going. Mr. Thomas Dale, who carries on business as a greengrocer, asked for the exemption of his only assistant, a married man, aged 30 years, with one child.

. Captain Mathams pointed out that he had already had a term off and the Tribunal refused the application, the Chairman remarking that a man of thirty years was wanted in the Army. Mr. Dale: It simply breaks up my business. It is like amputating the right arm of an old man.
The Chairman: Well, I llope it isn't as bad as that.
Applicant Protests.

Because he was only given a month's exemp- tion a master window-cleaner '(married and having two children) uttered a protest. "A paltry month!" he exclaimed. - "You have given one man conditional exempt on and he has not been in the business more than two years. Another you have given three months, and me a month!"
Captain Mathams: You can appeal to Liver- pool. The Chairman: It is hardly fair to make an accusation against us when the cases may not be on all fours.
The applicant was about to say something more when the Chairman stopped him with the remark: "I am not here to argue with you." • Off-Licence Special Case.

Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, appealed on behalf of a grocer and off-licensee, aged 41 years next month, whose wife and boy, aged 10, are ill. "It is not like cases where you can trans- fer the licence to the wife," urged Mr. Browne. Two months' exemption. " Most Reprehensible."
A draper, married, who had had a temporary exemption. admitted that since the last hearing he had increased his stock, also his indebted- ness.
Captain 3fathams: It is really equivalent to "bouncing" the Tribunal. It is most repre- hensible cqnduct, when you were given exemp- tion with the object of disposing of your busi- ness.
The Chairman: You also entered into .your lease after the war started.'
Two month' further exemption—final.

div.head: CHESHIRE SIDE.
div.p: THE CHESHIRE SIDE.
Stockton Heath And Grappen-
hall Cases Hearth

Many cases from Stockton Heath and Grap- penhall appeared on the list for consideration by Runcorn Rural District Local Tribunal on Thursday. A Stockton Heath fish and fruit dealer, aged 30, married, and who has been established in business for 121 years, asked for exemption. Time had been already extended in his case until Ist August. In reply to the Chairman, he said that the conditions now existing were practically the same as when he first applied. The appeal was refused. "1 Wish I Had Been a Farmer's Son."

A Stdckton Heath hairdresser and tobacconist applied for a renewal of exemption which had been originally granted until Ist August. Applicant is 32 years of age, married, one child, and has been in business for twelve years. When the Chairman informed applicant that his appeal was refused the latter remarked " Ridiculous—l wish I had been a farmer's son." •
The Runcorn Rural District Council applied for exemption .on behalf of one of their in- spectors of nuisances, who resides at Stockton Heath.
Exemption was granted until Ist October.

A house painter-, of Lower Walton, aged 38, married, appealed for exemption on domestic grounds. His wife is in delicate health. The case was 'adjourned for fourteen days in order that applicant should get work with a firm making munitions. Mr. John Bradford, Grappenhall, applied for exemption for a teamsman, aged 26, married, three children. He had also a man ?() years, exempted until November, and a head teams- man, 39. He recently had five or six children picking potatoes. The case was adjourned for inquiries. Mr. Bradford asked if the Tribunal was dealing with his son's application. He had met with an accident.

The Clerk (Mr. Hough) said the case did not appear on the list. A single man aged 23, described as a farmer at Grappenhall, whose father is 83 years old, was granted exemption until Ist November. It transpired that another young man, aged 25, is employed on the farm. A Grappenhall farmer appealed on behalf of his son, aged 22 years, unmarried, who works as ploughman and teamsman on a farm of 70 acres. It transpired that there was another son of military age on the farm, and the present case was adjourned until the application in ro- gard to the other son came before the Tribunal. A Thelwall farmer appealed on behalf of his son (25), who is employed as teamsman. He has also two boys, 14 or 15.

aged 45, has -indifferent health, and can only help on the farm sometimes. Exemption had been granted for a teamsman for whom he had appealed, and who is 24 years of age. The farm is one of 106 acres. Conditional exemption granted.

A Whitley lady applied for exemption for her son, aged 24, single, who acts in the capacities of cowman and farm bailiff, having to look after 100 acres of land and 30 head of cattle. Conditional exemption granted.

Mr: David Bradburn, Who is 75 years of age, and has a. farm of 113 acres ,at Lower Whitley, appealed on behalf of his teamsman, a married man, aged 39 years, and who has a family of six children. Conditional exemption_ was voted.

Mr. Arthur Browne, Solicitor, applied for con- ditional exemption for Mr. Robert 'Warburton, farmer, of Bank House Farm, Thelviall, on the ground that their farm consisted of 170 acres, with six horses and 30 milking cows, and the only males on the farm were the three brothers, and no other help whatever, and that they had got in 50 acres of hay, and•there were 40 acres of corn still to be harvested. In addition to this they had 35 tons of straw to .deliver to the military authorities within the next ten days, and it would all have to be carted to Warring- ton. .
The Tribunal granted•exemption until the Ist October, but the •Chairman intimated that if, any fuither time were wanted leave would be required for any further hearing.
