div.head: CHARLES DUKES
div.p: CHARLES DUKES
Loses A Further Conscience Appeal At Manchester.
JUDGE'S CROSS-EXAMINA- TION.

Mr. Charles Dukes, who appealed for and was refused exemption from military service at the Salford Hundred Appeal Court, at Manchester, on Tuesday afternoon, had against -him in the chair that brilliant cross-examiner, his Honour Judge Mellor, K.C. The quick-wittedness of the Chairman and the resolve of Mr. Dukes to counter the thrusts and make the best of his case, provided a quarter of an hour's most interesting dialogue. On the applicant taking his seat Captain Murphy said the military authorities wished to take no part in the ease, being content to leave it entirely to the discretion of the Tribunal. The Chairman then read Mr. Dukes' appeal as follows :—" I desire to appeal against the decision of the local Tribunal, who rejected my appeal on the grounds that my convictions were political rather than moral. I hold the opposite opinion. With me war is not a question of political expediency, neither do I agree that it is possible to justify war politically whilst dis- agreeing with war morally. My convictions are based upon the moral concept that in the right and wrong of social progress war is never justi• fiable. My political views and activities are a consequence of my moral views and not some- times separate and apart from them." The Chairman is exceedingly speedy-minded and, having read the foregoing at about 200 words a minute, he fired the following question at Mr. Dukes without heeding the full stop, "But what are moral views? I don't quite know what moral views mean."
The Applicant: I have supplied testimony as to the long duration I have held these views regarding war. _ _ _
The Chairman: But what are the views? You say they are moral views. Upon what are they founded—upon something religious, or what?
Applicant: No, they are based upon my moral abhorrence of anything in the nature of—
The Chairman: But what are your moral views? Morality is founded on religion of some sort or kind. Do you found your objection on that, or is your objection against conscription or what?

Applicant: No, my objection is to every form of war, and it is the result of my own thinking out. I am not a member of any religioua sect. I have not gone to anyone else to define my views for me. They are the result of my own thinking, and personally I could not take part in any form of war whatever. I made that clear on other occasions, and I offered as an alternative, realising that one has to do some- thing, to accept any form of alternative service. The Chairman: What would you do?

Applicant: Anything in a civil capacity: anything of any, kind the Tribunal care to formulate for me. I leave it there. Well, but you see you are a gentleman who likes to make a fuss about things. Suppose we sent you to one particular thing, you might find something wrong—or what you supposed was wrong—connected either with the work- neople or the working of the thing and chuck it over?-1 don't think my past would give any indication of that. • "Fairly Well-known." •

I don't know; I don't want to say anything about it, but you are fairly well-known in this district.—Yes, I believe I am, and I believe that my record simply goes to testify to the views I am now putting before this Tribunal. But what you say you are entitled to is an exemption from military service on the ground of conscience. Conscience must be more or less founded on some religious ideas of some sort. The ordinary meaning of the word con- science is that it is founded on some sort of moral conception or some religious tenet. If, on the other hand, you are only a person who •19jects to war—and we all object to it—that is not what I may call conscience?—May I put it. in this way? , I Yam a Socialist of some little note. I have taken part in, the formation of Socialist societies, one of the main planks of which is the building up of an international fraternity of the workers. Well, you don't tell me that Socialists object to fighting?—l don't say they all do. No, very few do.—There are a very consider- able number who do. I am one of those who do object. I submit again that I have supplied testimony of my convictions. There is none of it here?—There might not be, but I sent it in along with the appeal. The extraordinary part of it is, why was it that you put in other appeals before you thought of your conscience ?—That is not quite correct. If you will permit me just a moment to explain—l don't want there to be any error in this—l put in an appeal on. conscientious grounds on the same date and at the same time that the Union, which is my employer, put in its appeal. I have a receipt for it. I was asked not to put in a personal appeal. Why didn't they want you to appeal?—The Union believed I should stand a far better chance of exemption if I did, not put in an appeal on conscientious grounds. I was not prepared to do that. For some reason best known to somebody here, they claimed to have lost trace of my original appeal, but on the last occasion I brought along the receipt for that with me.

The Chairman: Have you got it here ?—I have not brought it here.l have just come down from Colne, where I have been dealing with a big labour dispute, and one does not carry these things about with one. The Chairman: This is your own matter. We cannot help it.. We must have something or other, because you say that your original appeal was lost. It has been suggested—you say wrongly—that this conscientious objection on your part is a second string, that you have already been to two or three Tribunals on the other question and then you. find this. Applicant: Are you prepared to defer the matter for a day and I will produce the receipt? Captain Murphy having left the room, Mr. Clay, solicitor, was present on behalf of the military, and intervened with the remark: The only part I want to take is that we submit that the conscientious ground Mr. Dukes has put down is not the conscientious ground con- templated by the Act of Parliament. We quite admit he has put in his claim. We do no dis- pute that. The Chairman: I understood the first claim was made by the Union. It was refused by the Tribunal below and then they annealed to the Tribunal above and they also refused it. Then Mr. Clynes came down here, representing the Union, and asked for a re-hearing. The appeal was re-heard and again refused. Then I understand Mr. Dukes put in the conscientious appeal. The Applicant: That is not correct. Mr. Clay: The Tribunal .below disallowed his conscientious appeal on the ground that the conscientious exclusion clause in the Act of Parliament did not apply to such an objection as his.
